root.stem: A 66-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of right-sided weakness and inability to speak. She has had rheumatic mitral stenosis since childhood. The right side of her face droops below the eye with the forehead spared, her right hand and forearm are weaker than her right leg, and she coughs when she tries to swallow water. She follows commands and understands what is said to her, but she cannot repeat words or answer questions. Her pulse is irregularly irregular at 118/min, and an electrocardiogram (ECG) shows no P waves. She has no headache, vomiting or seizure, her vision is normal, and a computed tomography (CT) scan of the head shows no blood.
root.oneliner: 66F + sudden right face, hand and arm weakness 2 hours ago + forehead spared + cannot repeat or answer but understands + swallowing trouble + rheumatic mitral stenosis + irregularly irregular pulse, no P waves + no headache, vomiting or seizure + normal vision + no blood on CT
highlight: right hand and forearm are weaker than her right leg
coughs when she tries to swallow water
understands what is said to her

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Brain tissue dies because an artery is blocked. The clincher: **sudden one-sided weakness with loss of speech in a woman with atrial fibrillation, and no blood on CT**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The exam often says cerebral infarction. The older term cerebrovascular accident (CVA) is broader: it also covers intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhage.

nodes.q: Where did the blocking clot most likely form?
nodes.a: In the left atrial appendage (cardioembolic stroke)
nodes.note: In atrial fibrillation (AF) the atrium quivers instead of contracting, so blood pools and clots, mostly in the left atrial appendage; rheumatic mitral stenosis enlarges the atrium and adds to the stasis. The clot passes through the left ventricle and aorta, up the internal carotid artery, into the brain.

nodes.q: Which artery is blocked?
nodes.note: The middle cerebral artery (MCA) is the direct continuation of the internal carotid, so emboli land there most often. Right-sided signs mean a left-hemisphere lesion. The clincher: **face and hand weaker than leg + aphasia**. Its lenticulostriate branches also supply the internal capsule.

nodes.q: Why are her face and hand weaker than her leg?
nodes.a: The face and hand areas of the motor cortex lie on the lateral surface supplied by this artery; the leg area lies on the medial surface and is spared
nodes.note: The cortical map of the body (motor homunculus) is folded so that the leg lies along the midline.

nodes.q: If the same kind of stroke had weakened her left hand and forearm instead, which artery would be blocked?
nodes.note: Motor fibers cross in the lower medulla, so weakness appears on the side opposite the lesion. Hand and forearm weakness points to the lateral convexity of the cortex.

nodes.q: She understands speech but cannot repeat words or answer questions. Which language problem is this?
nodes.note: The lesion is in the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area) of the dominant hemisphere, the left in nearly all right-handed people, supplied by the superior division of the middle cerebral artery. Comprehension is spared; she knows her speech is wrong. An inferior-division lesion (superior temporal gyrus) would instead give fluent speech with poor comprehension (Wernicke aphasia).

nodes.q: The forehead is spared in her facial droop. Which type of motor neuron lesion explains this?
nodes.a: An upper motor neuron lesion in the hemisphere opposite the weak side
nodes.note: The forehead muscles receive input from both hemispheres, so only the lower face droops. A lower motor neuron lesion, such as a facial nerve palsy, weakens the forehead too. The limbs are first limp, then become spastic with brisk reflexes over days to weeks.

nodes.q: Which neurotransmitter, released by neurons dying from the lack of oxygen, kills the neurons around the infarct?
nodes.note: Excess glutamate overstimulates N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, calcium floods the cells, and enzymes digest them (excitotoxicity). The rim of at-risk tissue around the dead core is the penumbra.

nodes.q: A drug that blocks the NMDA receptor would have which direct effect on neurons?
nodes.note: This is the aim of neuroprotective drugs; none has yet improved outcomes in people.

nodes.q: Which kind of necrosis does infarcted brain tissue undergo?
nodes.note: Brain is rich in lipid and digestive enzymes and has little supporting connective tissue, so dead tissue turns to fluid. Timeline: **red (eosinophilic) neurons at 12 to 24 hours**, neutrophils at 1 to 3 days, microglia and macrophages from about day 3 to 5, reactive astrocytes and new vessels from 1 to 2 weeks, and a glial scar with a fluid-filled cyst after 2 weeks to months.

nodes.q: Six months later, which cell type has proliferated around the healed lesion?
nodes.note: Macrophages clear the debris and leave a fluid-filled cavity ringed by astrocytic scar (gliosis); the brain does not scar with fibroblasts.

nodes.q: Eight years later, a brain-stem section on the side of the infarct would show what?
nodes.note: Wallerian degeneration of the corticospinal fibers whose cell bodies were destroyed; the crus cerebri carries them through the midbrain.

nodes.q: Which deficit did that tract damage cause during life?
nodes.a: Spastic weakness of the limbs on the side opposite the shrunken crus cerebri
nodes.note: The corticospinal fibers cross in the caudal medulla, below the midbrain, so a lesion above the crossing weakens the opposite side. Cerebellar and joint-position signs do not come from this tract.

nodes.q: Which complication of a large infarct peaks 3 to 5 days later and can kill?
nodes.note: Dead tissue swells (cytotoxic edema) and shifts the brain under the falx and down through the tentorium. Uncal herniation compresses the oculomotor nerve (a dilated pupil on the same side) and the brainstem. It is the leading cause of early death after large middle cerebral artery infarcts; decompressive hemicraniectomy can save life.

nodes.q: Bleeding into the dead tissue days later is more common with her type of stroke than with a stroke from a clot formed in place. What is this complication called?
nodes.note: The embolus breaks up, blood flow returns into vessels damaged by ischemia, and they leak, giving a red (hemorrhagic) infarct. Fibrinolytics raise the risk. Thrombotic infarcts are usually pale.

nodes.q: Which drug class would best improve her weakness over the next few hours?
nodes.note: Tissue plasminogen activators (tPA) convert plasminogen to plasmin, which cuts fibrin and dissolves the clot so the penumbra can recover. Their main danger is bleeding, especially inside the skull.

nodes.q: Within how many hours of the onset of symptoms must the fibrinolytic be started?
nodes.note: She is at 2 hours, so she qualifies. A noncontrast CT of the head must first exclude bleeding; blood pressure must be below 185/110 mm Hg, and recent bleeding, major surgery or a low platelet count rule it out. If the time of onset is unknown, the last time she was seen normal counts.

nodes.q: Which procedure removes a clot from a large proximal artery, even up to 24 hours after onset in selected patients?
nodes.note: Used when vessel imaging shows a large vessel occlusion; fibrinolysis is still given first if she qualifies.

nodes.q: Which long-term drug best prevents another embolus when atrial fibrillation occurs with rheumatic mitral stenosis?
nodes.note: A vitamin K antagonist, aiming for an international normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 3. Direct oral anticoagulants are not used in moderate to severe rheumatic mitral stenosis, and aspirin alone is not enough. After a large infarct, anticoagulation is usually delayed for several days to limit hemorrhagic transformation.

nodes.q: If she had been in sinus rhythm with a bruit over the left side of her neck, where would the embolus most likely have come from?
nodes.a: An atherosclerotic plaque at the bifurcation of the left common carotid artery (internal carotid artery stenosis)
nodes.note: Platelet-fibrin debris breaks off the plaque and travels to the middle cerebral artery (artery-to-artery embolism). A small embolus to the ophthalmic artery causes amaurosis fugax: brief one-eyed blindness, like a shade coming down.

nodes.q: Carotid duplex ultrasonography shows 80% narrowing of that artery. Which procedure lowers her risk of another stroke?
nodes.note: Offered within about 2 weeks for a symptomatic stenosis of 70% to 99% (and selected cases of 50% to 69%), together with antiplatelet therapy and a high-intensity statin. Carotid stenting is an alternative when surgery is risky.

nodes.q: Sudden one-sided weakness could suggest intracerebral hemorrhage. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Headache, vomiting and very high blood pressure, with bright white blood on CT**; usually rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of the lenticulostriate arteries in long-standing hypertension
**No headache or vomiting + no blood on CT + a source of emboli (atrial fibrillation)**

nodes.note: The trap: the weakness looks identical and only CT separates them; a fibrinolytic given to a bleed is harmful.

nodes.q: Her weakness could suggest an anterior cerebral artery stroke. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Leg and foot weaker than arm and face + abulia (lack of will) + urinary incontinence**; the artery supplies the medial surface of the hemisphere

split.a: Ischemic stroke of the middle cerebral artery
split.note: **Face and hand weaker than leg + aphasia**

nodes.q: Her weakness could suggest a lacunar stroke. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pure motor weakness of face, arm and leg equally, with no aphasia or other cortical signs**; a small deep infarct of the internal capsule from hyaline arteriolosclerosis (lipohyalinosis) of the lenticulostriate arteries in long-standing hypertension or diabetes

split.a: Ischemic stroke of the middle cerebral artery
split.note: **Aphasia + hand weaker than leg + an embolic source**

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from the case
rows: **Opposite-side loss of half of the visual field, with the center of vision spared (macular sparing)**
**Thunderclap headache (worst of life) with blood around the brain on CT**
No headache and no blood on CT
**Deficit that clears completely, usually within an hour**
Her deficit has lasted 2 hours and persists

head: Look-alike

rows: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, posterior inferior cerebellar artery

**Vertigo, nystagmus, hoarseness and dysphagia (nucleus ambiguus) + same-side Horner syndrome and facial pain-temperature loss + opposite-side body pain-temperature loss + same-side ataxia**; no limb weakness

root.stem: A 35-year-old woman has had 2 months of generalized weakness that gets worse through the day. By evening she has double vision and her eyelids droop. Her arm strength falls with repeated shoulder raises but recovers after a short rest. Her deep tendon reflexes are normal, sensation is intact, her pupils react normally, and she has no dry mouth. She does not smoke. After a trial dose of pyridostigmine, her strength improves within the hour.
root.oneliner: 35F + 2 months of weakness worse through the day + evening double vision and ptosis + arm fatigue with repetition, recovers with rest + normal reflexes, normal pupils, no dry mouth, nonsmoker + improves within the hour after pyridostigmine
highlight: falls with repeated shoulder raises but recovers after a short rest

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction. The clincher: **weakness that worsens with repeated use and improves with rest, affecting the eyes first, with normal reflexes and a quick response to pyridostigmine**.

nodes.q: Antibodies against which protein cause the weakness?
nodes.a: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor on the muscle end plate
nodes.note: A type II hypersensitivity reaction: the IgG antibodies block the receptors, speed their removal and fix complement that damages the end plate, so each nerve impulse produces a smaller muscle response, and the response falls further with repetition. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows this as a decremental response.

nodes.q: A neoplasm linked to this disease would most likely be found in which organ?
nodes.note: Thymic hyperplasia with germinal centers is found in most patients with receptor antibodies; a thymoma, an anterior mediastinal mass seen on chest computed tomography, in about 10% to 15%. The thymus is thought to start the autoimmune response.

nodes.q: Which blood test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Serum antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor
nodes.note: If negative, test for antibodies against muscle-specific kinase (MuSK). Single-fiber electromyography is the most sensitive electrical test, and a chest computed tomography scan looks for thymoma.

nodes.q: Which bedside test, needing no drug, briefly lifts her drooping eyelid?
nodes.note: Ice held over the closed eye for about 2 minutes slows acetylcholinesterase, so more acetylcholine reaches the receptors and the ptosis improves by 2 mm or more.

nodes.q: How does the drug she was given improve her strength?
nodes.a: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so more acetylcholine stays in the synaptic cleft to act on the remaining nicotinic receptors
nodes.note: Pyridostigmine is a quaternary amine that does not enter the brain and is the main symptomatic treatment. Neostigmine works the same way. Muscarinic side effects (cramps, diarrhea, sweating) are blocked with glycopyrrolate.

nodes.q: Which very short-acting drug of the same class was once given intravenously to confirm the diagnosis within a minute?
nodes.note: The Tensilon test: strength returns for a few minutes. It also separated a myasthenic crisis (improves) from a cholinergic crisis (worsens). It is no longer marketed in the United States, but it is still tested.

nodes.q: Which operation is advised when a thymoma is found, and for many younger patients with generalized disease and receptor antibodies?
nodes.note: Thymectomy reduces symptoms and steroid needs. Prednisone, azathioprine or other immunosuppressants are added if symptoms persist.

nodes.q: She doubles her pyridostigmine dose and becomes weaker with trouble breathing. Which change at the receptor explains the new weakness?
nodes.a: Desensitization of nicotinic receptors by excess acetylcholine
nodes.note: This is a cholinergic crisis: too much acetylcholine keeps the end plate depolarized, so the receptors stop responding (a depolarizing block, like succinylcholine).

nodes.q: Her new weakness could also be a myasthenic crisis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Worse weakness after an infection or a missed dose, with no muscarinic signs**; improves with more acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (and once did with edrophonium)

**Weakness after a higher dose + muscarinic excess: small pupils, salivation, sweating, diarrhea, slow heart rate, wheezing**; worsens with more drug, treat by stopping it and giving atropine for the muscarinic signs

nodes.note: The trap: both cause breathing failure in a treated patient. Whatever the cause, protect the airway first.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening complication of the disease itself weakens the breathing muscles?
nodes.note: Infection, surgery, pregnancy, and drugs such as aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium and beta-blockers can trigger it. Death comes from respiratory failure, often with aspiration from bulbar weakness.

nodes.q: Which treatment physically removes the circulating antibodies?
nodes.note: Intravenous immunoglobulin is the alternative and works about as fast. Follow forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, and intubate early if they fall.

nodes.q: If she becomes pregnant, why might her newborn have a weak cry and poor sucking for a few weeks?
nodes.a: Her IgG antibodies cross the placenta and block the baby's receptors (transient neonatal myasthenia)
nodes.note: It fades over weeks as maternal IgG is cleared. It shows the disease is antibody-mediated.

nodes.q: Her fatigable weakness could suggest Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Proximal leg weakness that improves with repeated effort + absent reflexes + dry mouth**; antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels, often with small cell lung cancer in smokers
**Eye and bulbar weakness that worsens with repeated effort + normal reflexes**; antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors

nodes.note: The trap: both are fatigable neuromuscular junction diseases.

nodes.q: Her double vision could suggest botulism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Descending paralysis with dilated, poorly reactive pupils and dry mouth** after improperly canned food or, in infants, honey; toxin blocks acetylcholine release
**Fatigable weakness with normal pupils and no dry mouth; better with rest**

nodes.q: Other causes of weakness were also possible. Which finding in her case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from the case
rows: **Ascending symmetric weakness with absent reflexes after an infection**
Normal reflexes and weakness that varies through the day
**Relapsing deficits separated in time and space, with brisk reflexes**
Normal reflexes, no upper motor neuron signs, and improvement with rest

root.stem: A 70-year-old woman is found pulseless at home by her husband, and paramedics restore a heartbeat after 15 minutes of resuscitation. In the emergency department she is stuporous with a temperature of 37.0°C. Her pupils are 2 mm and react to light, her eyes move fully with cold-water caloric testing, and she withdraws both arms and both legs symmetrically to pain. She has no history of alcohol use, and her blood glucose is normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain shows abnormal signal in both medial temporal lobes.
root.oneliner: 70F + found pulseless at home, heartbeat back after 15 minutes of resuscitation + stuporous, afebrile + reactive 2-mm pupils, full eye movements on calorics, symmetric withdrawal to pain + no alcohol, normal glucose + bilateral medial temporal lobe signal on MRI
highlight: eyes move fully with cold-water caloric testing
withdraws both arms and both legs symmetrically

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Brain damage from too little blood flow or oxygen, here after a cardiac arrest. The clincher: **reduced consciousness with working brainstem reflexes after a period without circulation, and symmetric hippocampal signal change**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also called anoxic or hypoxic encephalopathy. Global means the whole brain is underperfused, as in cardiac arrest or profound hypotension; focal ischemia is a stroke.

nodes.q: Which part of the brain do her reactive pupils and full eye movements on caloric testing show is still working?
nodes.note: Brainstem neurons tolerate low oxygen better than cortical neurons, so the damage is mainly in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. Brain death would abolish these reflexes.

nodes.q: Which neurons are most vulnerable to a drop in oxygen, including after profound hypotension during an operation?
nodes.a: Pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus (the CA1 or Sommer sector)
nodes.note: Next most vulnerable are pyramidal neurons of cortical layers 3, 5 and 6 (laminar necrosis), and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. These cells have high energy demand and many glutamate receptors, so they die first.

nodes.q: Which microscopic change appears in these neurons 12 to 24 hours later?
nodes.a: Red neurons (shrunken, with eosinophilic cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei)
nodes.note: A sign of irreversible injury.

nodes.q: Two months later, which memory deficit would she have?
nodes.a: Inability to learn and recall new facts (anterograde amnesia)
nodes.note: The hippocampus stores new memories; old memories stay intact.

nodes.q: Between which arterial territories does a wedge-shaped infarct appear when blood pressure falls?
nodes.a: The border zones (watershed areas) between the major cerebral arteries
nodes.note: The border zone between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries is hit hardest, which weakens the proximal arms and thighs (the "man in a barrel"). Cortex and the white matter beneath it are affected.

nodes.q: If the cortex is largely destroyed but the brainstem survives, which outcome leaves her awake without awareness?
nodes.note: She has sleep-wake cycles but no awareness; brain death means loss of all brain and brainstem function.

nodes.q: Which treatment after resuscitation helps protect the brain of a comatose survivor?
nodes.note: Hold a constant temperature between 32 and 37.5°C for at least 24 hours, then prevent fever. Prognosis is judged at least 72 hours later with examination, electroencephalography, MRI and blood markers.

nodes.q: Her temporal lobe changes could suggest herpes simplex encephalitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, headache, seizures and behavior change over days; hemorrhagic, often asymmetric temporal lesions; herpes simplex virus DNA in cerebrospinal fluid**
**No fever + circulation lost for minutes + symmetric hippocampal and cortical signal**

nodes.note: The trap: both injure the medial temporal lobes.

nodes.q: Her stupor could suggest Wernicke encephalopathy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia with alcohol use or poor nutrition**; mammillary body lesions; improves with thiamine
**Cardiac arrest + full eye movements + hippocampal signal change**

nodes.q: Other causes were also possible. Which finding in her case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from the case
rows: **Memory loss that worsens gradually over years**
Lacunar infarcts of the basal ganglia
**Small deep infarcts from long-standing hypertension, causing pure motor or sensory loss**
Symmetric hippocampal change after loss of circulation
**Thunderclap headache with blood around the brain**

root.stem: A 17-year-old boy has fallen asleep several times a day in class for 18 months, each time for 10 to 15 minutes, and he wakes refreshed. The slightest noise wakes him. He sees vivid dreamlike scenes just as he falls asleep at night, and twice he has felt unable to move his legs for a minute after waking in the morning. He has never collapsed when laughing. His older brother also fell asleep often at school. He does not snore, does not drink alcohol, has a body mass index (BMI) of 22 kg/m2, and has a normal physical and neurologic examination.
root.oneliner: 17M + falls asleep several times a day for 18 months, short refreshing naps + wakes to the slightest noise + vivid dreams on falling asleep + brief leg paralysis on waking + no cataplexy + brother affected + no snoring, BMI 22
highlight: fallen asleep several times a day
vivid dreamlike scenes just as he falls asleep
unable to move his legs for a minute after waking

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A disorder of sleep-wake control. The clincher: **daytime sleep attacks with short refreshing naps + dreamlike hallucinations on falling asleep + brief paralysis on waking**.

nodes.q: Which feature that he lacks completes the classic tetrad of the disease?
nodes.a: Cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion)
nodes.note: The tetrad is daytime sleepiness, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis and cataplexy. Narcolepsy with cataplexy is type 1; without it, type 2.

nodes.q: How does his sleep begin at night, compared with a normal sleeper?
nodes.a: Directly from wakefulness into rapid eye movement (REM) sleep
nodes.note: Normal sleep passes through the non-REM stages first. The early REM bursts explain dreams on falling asleep, and the muscle paralysis of REM spilling into wakefulness explains the paralysis on waking.

nodes.q: Loss of neurons in the lateral hypothalamus that make which neuropeptide causes the classic form of the disease?
nodes.note: Autoimmune loss is suspected, with a strong link to the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) allele DQB1*06:02. Low orexin in cerebrospinal fluid defines type 1 (with cataplexy); in type 2, as in this boy, orexin is usually normal.

nodes.q: Which tests confirm the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
nodes.note: A short mean sleep latency (8 minutes or less) with at least two sleep-onset REM periods.

nodes.q: Which drug promoting wakefulness is first-line for the daytime sleepiness?
nodes.note: It mainly blocks dopamine reuptake. Armodafinil, amphetamine-type stimulants, solriamfetol and pitolisant are alternatives; sodium oxybate (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) helps cataplexy and night sleep.

nodes.q: Which behavioral measure helps alongside the drug?
nodes.a: Scheduled short naps with regular sleep times
nodes.note: He should also avoid driving when drowsy.

nodes.q: His daytime sleepiness could suggest obstructive sleep apnea. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Obesity, loud snoring and witnessed breathing pauses; unrefreshing sleep and morning headache**; improves with continuous positive airway pressure
**Thin, no snoring, short refreshing naps + hallucinations on falling asleep + paralysis on waking**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause sleep attacks in the daytime.

nodes.q: The vivid dreams could suggest REM sleep behavior disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Acts out dreams, with punching or shouting, because the muscle paralysis of REM is lost**; older men, later Parkinson disease
**Dreamlike hallucinations on falling asleep without acting them out + daytime sleep attacks**

nodes.q: Other sleep disorders were also possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from the case
rows: **Urge to move the legs at rest in the evening, relieved by movement**
**Child screams in deep non-REM sleep, cannot be comforted and does not remember**
Dreamlike scenes he remembers, and daytime sleep attacks
**Long unrefreshing naps and difficulty waking, without REM-onset sleep**
His naps are short and refreshing, with hallucinations and paralysis

root.stem: A 37-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection has had 3 weeks of severe leg pain and of pain, numbness and tingling in both feet. His regimen includes stavudine. The soles of his feet are tender to touch and pinprick sensation is decreased over both calves and feet. Ankle reflexes are reduced, strength is normal, and the symptoms are symmetric. His fasting glucose and vitamin B12 level are normal, and he does not drink alcohol.
root.oneliner: 37M + HIV on stavudine regimen + 3 weeks of leg pain and burning, numbness, tingling in both feet + tender soles + decreased pinprick over calves and feet, symmetric + normal strength + normal glucose and B12, no alcohol
highlight: soles of his feet are tender to touch
pinprick sensation is decreased over both calves and feet
fasting glucose and vitamin B12 level are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Damage to the longest sensory nerves. The clincher: **painful burning feet with symmetric loss of pinprick over the feet and calves in an HIV-infected man, with normal strength, glucose and vitamin B12**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same symmetric, length-dependent neuropathy.

nodes.q: Besides the virus itself, which antiretroviral group in his regimen can cause the same neuropathy?
nodes.a: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (stavudine, didanosine, zalcitabine)
nodes.note: The older "d-drugs" (stavudine, didanosine, zalcitabine) inhibit mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, causing mitochondrial toxicity and axonal damage. They are now rarely used.

nodes.q: If one of these drugs is the cause, what is the first management step?
nodes.a: Switch to a less neurotoxic antiretroviral drug
nodes.note: Symptoms may briefly worsen before they improve.

nodes.q: Which pattern of nerve damage explains why the feet are affected before the hands?
nodes.note: The longest axons fail first ("dying back"), giving a stocking distribution. Other treatable causes (diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, alcohol, other neurotoxic drugs) must be excluded first.

nodes.q: Which drug is most appropriate for long-term relief of his pain?
nodes.note: A tricyclic antidepressant that blocks norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake and strengthens descending pain inhibition. Gabapentin, pregabalin and duloxetine are alternatives; acetaminophen, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and opioids work poorly for nerve pain.

nodes.q: What can the loss of feeling in his feet lead to?
nodes.a: Unnoticed injuries that become infected foot ulcers
nodes.note: Daily foot inspection and well-fitting shoes protect him.

nodes.q: His burning feet could suggest diabetic neuropathy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Long-standing hyperglycemia with a raised hemoglobin A1c; often retinopathy and nephropathy as well**
**HIV infection and nucleoside drug exposure with normal glucose**

nodes.note: The trap: both give a painful stocking-distribution neuropathy.

nodes.q: His numbness could suggest vitamin B12 deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Loss of vibration and position sense with macrocytic anemia and spinal cord signs; raised methylmalonic acid**
**Burning pain and pinprick loss with a normal B12 level**

nodes.q: Other neuropathies were also possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from the case
rows: **Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency during tuberculosis treatment; prevented by giving pyridoxine**
**Ascending weakness over days with absent reflexes**
Normal strength and symptoms over weeks

root.stem: A 27-year-old man with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) has had 6 weeks of progressive memory loss, poor concentration, imbalance and clumsiness. He stopped combination antiretroviral therapy 3 months ago and recently recovered from Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. His CD4+ T-cell count is 60/mm3. He has no fever or headache and no focal weakness. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain shows symmetric white-matter hyperintensities in both hemispheres without mass effect or ring enhancement. A brain biopsy shows scattered nodules of small inflammatory cells containing multinucleated giant cells.
root.oneliner: 27M + AIDS, off antiretrovirals for 3 months + 6 weeks of memory loss, poor concentration, imbalance, clumsiness + CD4 60 + afebrile, no focal deficit + symmetric white-matter hyperintensities, no mass or ring enhancement + nodules of small cells with multinucleated giant cells
highlight: progressive memory loss, poor concentration, imbalance and clumsiness
stopped combination antiretroviral therapy 3 months ago
no fever or headache and no focal weakness
symmetric white-matter hyperintensities in both hemispheres without mass effect or ring enhancement

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A subcortical dementia caused by the virus in the brain. The clincher: **progressive forgetfulness, slowing and clumsiness in advanced AIDS, with symmetric white-matter change and multinucleated giant cells**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All three names describe the same disease.

cystic mass in the right cerebellar hemisphere with an enhancing nodule in its wall

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common brain tumor of children. The clincher: **cystic cerebellar mass with an enhancing mural nodule in a child**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same tumor.

nodes.q: This tumor arises from cells that normally do which job in the brain?
nodes.note: Astrocytes also buffer potassium and form the blood-brain barrier. Oligodendrocytes make central myelin, microglia are the phagocytes, and ependymal cells line the ventricles.

nodes.note: The cells stain for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP).

nodes.q: Which treatment is usually curative?

**Cystic hemispheric mass with an enhancing mural nodule**

highlight: tuft of hair in the midline of his lower back

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A closed defect of the vertebral arch. The clincher: **a hair tuft over the lumbar spine with missing spinous processes, no sac, and normal legs**. It is most common at L5 to S1.

nodes.q: Failure of which embryologic event leaves the vertebral arch open?
nodes.note: Sclerotome mesenchyme grows around the neural tube and forms the vertebral arches. The neural tube itself closed normally, so the cord and meninges are normal.

nodes.q: Which vitamin taken before conception lowers the risk of the open neural tube defects?
nodes.note: 400 micrograms daily for all women who could become pregnant; 4 mg if an earlier child was affected.

nodes.q: Which maternal blood test is usually normal in this closed defect but raised in open ones?
nodes.note: Skin covers the defect, so fetal protein does not leak into the amniotic fluid.

nodes.q: Which problem can appear in childhood as the spinal cord is stretched by growth?
nodes.note: Leg weakness, foot deformities and bladder dysfunction; magnetic resonance imaging shows a low-lying conus and surgery frees the cord.

nodes.q: How is it managed when there are no symptoms?
nodes.note: It is common and often found by chance on a radiograph.

nodes.q: A lumbar spinal defect could suggest myelomeningocele. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sac containing spinal cord or nerve roots, with leg weakness, bladder dysfunction, hydrocephalus and raised alpha-fetoprotein**; the neural tube failed to close
**No sac, intact skin, normal legs + hair tuft over the missing arch**

nodes.note: The trap: both are called spina bifida, but here the neural tube closed normally.

nodes.q: A spinal defect could suggest a meningocele. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Skin-covered sac of meninges and cerebrospinal fluid with no neural tissue; normal neurologic function**
**No sac at all, with a hair tuft over the open arch**

root.stem: A 66-year-old man has had slowly worsening handwriting and slowness of movement for 2 years. His wife notices a fine tremor of both hands that is present when his hands rest in his lap and fades when he reaches for a cup. His face shows little expression, his steps are short and shuffling, and he has difficulty starting to walk and stopping once he is moving. When he is pulled gently backward at the shoulders he takes several steps and nearly falls. His arms resist passive movement in a ratchet-like way. His head and voice are steady, his memory is intact, his eye movements are full in all directions, and he has no hallucinations, no writhing movements, and takes no antipsychotic drugs.

highlight: present when his hands rest in his lap
fades when he reaches for a cup
difficulty starting to walk and stopping
takes several steps and nearly falls

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A degenerative disorder of movement. The clincher: **slowness of movement (bradykinesia) with a resting tremor that fades on action, cogwheel rigidity and a shuffling gait, in an older adult who takes no dopamine-blocking drug**.

nodes.q: Which finding must be present to make the diagnosis, along with at least one other cardinal sign?
nodes.note: Remember TRAP: Tremor at rest (pill-rolling, 4 to 6 per second), Rigidity (cogwheel), Akinesia or bradykinesia, Postural instability. His small handwriting (micrographia) and masked face are bradykinesia; his near fall when pulled backward is postural instability.

nodes.q: What is the name of the ratchet-like resistance the examiner feels when moving his arm?
nodes.note: Rigidity from a tremor superimposed on increased tone; it is present in all directions of movement (lead-pipe when there is no tremor).

nodes.q: Which gait does he show?
nodes.a: Festinating (shuffling, short-stepped) gait with freezing at the start and the stop
nodes.note: Stooped posture, reduced arm swing, and turning en bloc. He cannot correct a push, so he falls backward (retropulsion).

nodes.q: Loss of which neurotransmitter causes his illness?
nodes.note: Dopamine normally helps start voluntary movement. Roughly 60 to 80 percent of the dopaminergic cells are gone before signs appear.

nodes.q: Which brain structure loses its neurons?
nodes.a: Substantia nigra (pars compacta) in the midbrain
nodes.note: On a labeled coronal section it is the dark band lowest and most medial in the midbrain: the putamen is lateral, the thalamus is above, and the subthalamic nucleus lies just above the nigra. In Parkinson disease the nigra looks pale because it loses its pigmented (neuromelanin) dopaminergic neurons, which project to the striatum (the nigrostriatal pathway).

nodes.q: Which protein forms the Lewy bodies seen in the surviving nigral neurons?
nodes.note: Round, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions. Alpha-synuclein is also the protein in Lewy body dementia. Tau (Alzheimer, Pick), amyloid (Alzheimer plaques) and prion protein are the wrong options.

nodes.q: How does losing these neurons slow his movement?
nodes.a: Less drive from the thalamus to the motor cortex (reduced direct pathway, increased indirect pathway)
nodes.note: Without dopamine the basal ganglia over-inhibit the thalamus. The subthalamic nucleus becomes overactive, which is why it is a target for deep brain stimulation.

nodes.q: A 25-year-old man who injected a homemade synthetic opioid becomes suddenly rigid and unable to move. Which contaminant destroys the same neurons?
nodes.note: MPTP (1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine) is turned by monoamine oxidase B into MPP+, a poison of mitochondrial complex I that selectively kills dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra (not the striatum, raphe or locus ceruleus). The patient feels "frozen".

nodes.q: Which drug, a dopamine precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier, is the most effective treatment for his motor symptoms?
nodes.note: Dopamine itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, but levodopa can, and DOPA decarboxylase turns it into dopamine in the surviving nigral terminals. Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) are an alternative in younger patients to delay motor complications.

nodes.q: Which property of carbidopa lets it block dopamine formation in the body but not in the brain?
nodes.a: It does not cross the blood-brain barrier
nodes.note: It inhibits DOPA decarboxylase only outside the brain. More levodopa reaches the brain, and less dopamine forms in the body, which lowers nausea, vomiting and orthostatic hypotension.

nodes.q: After years of treatment, his benefit wears off between doses and he swings between moving freely and freezing. What is this called?
nodes.note: A late complication of levodopa as nigral cells keep dying. Involuntary writhing movements (dyskinesias) at peak dose are the other late problem.

nodes.q: Which drug class blocks the breakdown of dopamine to DOPAC (3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid) in the brain and helps smooth these swings?
nodes.note: Selective for type B at usual doses, so the tyramine (cheese) reaction is rare; avoid with meperidine or serotonergic drugs (serotonin syndrome).

nodes.q: Which other drug class lengthens each levodopa dose by blocking its conversion to 3-O-methyldopa outside the brain?
nodes.note: Entacapone acts only in the periphery; tolcapone also enters the brain and can damage the liver.

nodes.q: Which drug class helps mainly the tremor in a younger patient by restoring the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the striatum?
nodes.note: Avoid in older adults: confusion, urinary retention, constipation. Amantadine (more dopamine release, NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor blockade) helps dyskinesias.

nodes.q: He takes extra doses of his dopamine agonist on his own. Which adverse effect is most likely?
nodes.note: Excess dopaminergic stimulation of the mesolimbic pathway; compulsive gambling and other impulse-control problems and orthostatic hypotension also occur. Depression and tardive dyskinesia are not caused by extra dopamine agonist.

nodes.q: His tremor could suggest essential tremor. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Action or postural tremor** of the hands, head and voice that is worse when reaching and better with alcohol or propranolol; no slowness, rigidity or shuffling
**Rest tremor that fades on reaching + slow movements + rigidity**; head and voice spared

nodes.note: The trap: both give a tremor of both hands in an older adult.

nodes.q: His slowness could suggest Lewy body dementia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dementia with visual hallucinations and fluctuating attention** appearing before or within 1 year of the parkinsonism
**Movement signs for years before any dementia**; his memory is intact and there are no hallucinations

nodes.q: His near fall could suggest progressive supranuclear palsy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Loss of voluntary vertical gaze (down first) + early backward falls + a stiff neck and axial rigidity**; little response to levodopa
**Full eye movements + asymmetric resting tremor + good response to levodopa**

nodes.q: His movement disorder could suggest Huntington disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Chorea (writhing, jerky movements) + dementia + psychiatric change** with autosomal dominant inheritance; atrophy of the caudate
**Too little movement, not too much**: rest tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity from nigral loss

nodes.q: A degenerative brain disease at his age could suggest Alzheimer disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Progressive memory loss first**, with loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert; amyloid plaques and tau tangles
**Movement slowing and rest tremor first** with intact memory; dopaminergic nigral neurons are lost

nodes.q: His parkinsonism could be drug-induced. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Symmetric rigidity and bradykinesia that began after starting an antipsychotic (haloperidol) or metoclopramide**, from dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway; nigral neurons are intact, and it improves within weeks to months of stopping the drug
**Loss of nigral neurons with no dopamine-blocking drug**; he takes no antipsychotic

root.stem: A 74-year-old man falls from a stepladder in his garage, strikes his head, and has a scalp laceration. He is alert in the emergency department, a neurologic examination is normal, and he goes home. Two days later his wife finds him drowsy and complaining of a headache. He now has mild weakness of the right arm and leg, brisk right-sided reflexes, and an upgoing great toe on the right. His left pupil is 1 mm larger than the right and reacts sluggishly. He takes aspirin daily. Computed tomography (CT) of the head shows a crescent-shaped collection of blood over the left cerebral hemisphere that crosses suture lines but not the midline.

highlight: drowsy and complaining of a headache
mild weakness of the right arm and leg
upgoing great toe on the right
crosses suture lines but not the midline

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Blood collecting under the dura after head injury. The clincher: **crescent-shaped blood that crosses suture lines on CT, with delayed drowsiness and one-sided weakness after a head injury**.

nodes.q: Between which two layers of the meninges does the blood collect?
nodes.a: Between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater
nodes.note: The dura is not attached at the sutures, so the blood spreads over the whole hemisphere as a crescent; only the dural folds (falx cerebri and tentorium) stop it, which is why it does not cross the midline. Fresh blood is bright on CT; after about 2 weeks it becomes isodense, then dark (hypodense).

nodes.q: Which vessels were torn?
nodes.a: Bridging veins that cross from the cerebral cortex to the dural venous sinuses
nodes.note: Shearing from sudden head movement (acceleration-deceleration) tears them, and the low-pressure venous bleeding explains the delay of hours to days. Aspirin, anticoagulants and alcohol raise the risk. In an infant, a subdural hematoma with retinal hemorrhages points to shaken baby syndrome.

nodes.q: Why do these veins tear more easily at his age?
nodes.a: Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins across a wider subdural space
nodes.note: The same holds for chronic alcohol use and dementia.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening event follows a large collection?
nodes.note: Mass effect pushes the temporal lobe over the tentorium and the cingulate gyrus under the falx.

nodes.q: His left pupil is larger and reacts sluggishly. Which cranial nerve is being compressed?
nodes.a: The left oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III), by the herniating uncus
nodes.note: Its outer parasympathetic fibers are hit first, so the pupil dilates before the eye turns down and out. Next come decorticate then decerebrate posturing.

nodes.q: As the brainstem is pushed downward, which bleeding into the pons and midbrain causes death?
nodes.note: The midbrain and pons shift down while the basilar artery stays fixed, so its paramedian branches stretch and tear.

nodes.q: What is the treatment of a large, symptomatic collection with midline shift?
nodes.note: Small, asymptomatic collections are watched with repeat CT. Reverse anticoagulants.

nodes.q: While he waits for surgery, which ventilator change briefly lowers his intracranial pressure?
nodes.note: A short-term bridge only: its effect fades within hours, and too much can cause ischemia.

nodes.q: How does it lower the pressure?
nodes.a: Low arterial carbon dioxide causes cerebral vasoconstriction, which reduces cerebral blood volume
nodes.note: Cerebral blood flow falls with each drop in carbon dioxide, so the brain swells less.

nodes.q: If the bleeding is slow, weeks later an older person may show only confusion or headache. What does the collection look like on CT by then?
nodes.a: Crescent that has become hypodense (dark) compared with brain
nodes.note: A chronic subdural hematoma, often after a trivial fall that was forgotten.

nodes.q: His lucid period could suggest an epidural hematoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lens-shaped (biconvex) collection that stops at the sutures**, from the middle meningeal artery torn by a temporal bone fracture; rapid deterioration within hours
**Crescent-shaped collection that crosses sutures**, from torn bridging veins; slower, over hours to days, in the elderly

nodes.note: The trap: both can have a lucid period after a head blow.

nodes.q: His headache could suggest subarachnoid hemorrhage. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden worst headache of life with neck stiffness**; blood fills the basal cisterns and sulci from a ruptured berry aneurysm
**Gradual drowsiness after trauma + crescent over the hemisphere**

nodes.q: His one-sided weakness could suggest an intracerebral hemorrhage. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bleeding inside the brain tissue** (often the putamen) in a patient with severe hypertension
**Blood outside the brain** in a crescent under the dura after trauma

root.stem: A 55-year-old man with a 15-year history of hypertension that he treats irregularly develops a sudden severe headache and vomiting while lifting boxes at work. Over the next two hours he develops weakness of the right arm and leg and then becomes drowsy. His blood pressure is 220/125 mm Hg. Computed tomography (CT) of the head without contrast shows a bright, rounded 4-cm collection deep in the left hemisphere in the putamen, with surrounding swelling. The next evening his pulse falls to 50/min, his breathing becomes irregular, and his blood pressure rises further.
root.oneliner: 55M + 15 years of poorly treated hypertension + sudden severe headache and vomiting + right weakness then drowsiness + BP 220/125 + bright 4-cm putamen collection on CT + next day slow pulse, irregular breathing, rising BP

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Bleeding directly into brain tissue. The clincher: **sudden headache and vomiting with focal weakness progressing to coma in a patient with severe hypertension, and bright blood in the basal ganglia on CT**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both are forms of hemorrhagic stroke, which also includes subarachnoid hemorrhage; the deep hypertensive bleed is the classic intraparenchymal type.

nodes.q: What is the most common cause?
nodes.note: Other causes: amyloid angiopathy, anticoagulants, arteriovenous malformation, tumor, and cocaine.

nodes.q: Which artery usually ruptures in a deep bleed?
nodes.a: A lenticulostriate artery (a small penetrating branch of the middle cerebral artery)
nodes.note: Lenticulostriate arteries are small penetrating branches of the middle cerebral artery that supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Hypertensive bleeds favor the putamen (most common), thalamus, pons and cerebellum. A bridging vein (subdural), an arteriovenous malformation or a saccular aneurysm (subarachnoid) are the wrong options.

nodes.q: Which change in the vessel wall predisposes to rupture?
nodes.note: Chronic hypertension damages the walls of these small penetrating vessels (lipohyalinosis), and small outpouchings form that can rupture.

nodes.q: What do his later slow pulse, irregular breathing and rising blood pressure show?
nodes.a: The Cushing reflex of raised intracranial pressure
nodes.note: A response to brainstem compression.

nodes.q: Which event ends in death if the pressure keeps rising?
nodes.a: Downward herniation that compresses the medulla
nodes.note: The brain is pushed through the tentorial notch and the cerebellar tonsils into the foramen magnum, compressing the centers for breathing and circulation.

nodes.q: In an older adult, his bleed could suggest cerebral amyloid angiopathy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lobar bleed near the cortex in an older normotensive patient**, often recurrent; beta-amyloid in cortical vessel walls (apple-green birefringence with Congo red)
**Deep bleed in the putamen + long-standing hypertension**

nodes.q: What is the main treatment?
nodes.a: Lower the blood pressure and reverse any anticoagulant; no thrombolytics
nodes.note: Surgical removal is for cerebellar bleeds causing brainstem compression or hydrocephalus.

nodes.q: His weakness could suggest an ischemic stroke. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **CT without bright blood** (a dark wedge appears later); onset without headache or vomiting; thrombolysis may be given
**Bright blood on CT + headache, vomiting and rapid drowsiness** in severe hypertension; thrombolysis is contraindicated

nodes.note: The trap: weakness of one side comes the same way; only non-contrast CT of the head separates them, and it must come before any clot-dissolving drug.

nodes.q: His headache could suggest a ruptured saccular aneurysm. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Thunderclap headache with neck stiffness**; blood in the basal cisterns, often from the anterior communicating artery; strength usually normal at first
**Focal weakness + deep blood within the putamen** in hypertension

nodes.q: A young patient with the same bleed might suggest an arteriovenous malformation. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Young adult with seizures or a prior bleed; tangle of vessels** (flow voids); no long-standing hypertension
**Middle-aged patient + severe chronic hypertension + deep bleed**

nodes.q: The bright blood could suggest a subdural hematoma from bridging veins. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Crescent-shaped blood outside the brain after trauma**, from bridging veins
**Round blood inside the brain tissue with no head injury**

His neck flexors are weak, both legs are weaker than his arms, his knee and ankle reflexes are absent, and vibration and joint position sense are reduced at the fingertips and feet. He has been anxious about his thesis defense next month. He has no fever, his weakness is symmetric, there is no sensory level, his bladder works normally, and his weakness does not worsen with repeated effort. His pulse varies between 55 and 120/min, and his forced vital capacity is 2.1 L, down from 3.4 L last week.

vibration and joint position sense are reduced
does not worsen with repeated effort

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An acute autoimmune attack on peripheral nerves. The clincher: **symmetric ascending weakness with absent reflexes, days to weeks after an infection**.

nodes.q: Which kind of process in the peripheral nerves causes his weakness?
nodes.note: Immune attack (macrophages and antibodies) strips the myelin from peripheral nerves and roots, slowing or blocking conduction. It is a polyneuropathy: weakness plus loss of position sense with a normal bladder, which rules out anterior horn cell loss, muscle fiber degeneration, a neuromuscular junction disorder or a spinal cord lesion.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name that describes this injury. What is it?
nodes.note: The most common form in the US and Europe; axonal variants (acute motor axonal neuropathy) are rarer.

nodes.q: Which nerve fibers carry the vibration and position sense that he has lost?
nodes.note: Loss in both hands and both feet fits a peripheral nerve process, not one spinal cord column (the fasciculus gracilis carries only the legs, the fasciculus cuneatus only the arms). Large myelinated fibers depend most on myelin; small unmyelinated fibers (pain, temperature) are relatively spared.

nodes.q: Which bacterium most often causes the diarrhea that precedes it?
nodes.note: Its surface molecules resemble nerve gangliosides, so antibodies cross-react (molecular mimicry). Other triggers: cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and vaccination.

nodes.q: Which complication is the main cause of death?
nodes.a: Respiratory failure from weakness of the breathing muscles
nodes.note: Weakness can climb to involve the diaphragm within days.

nodes.q: Which bedside measurement tracks this risk?
nodes.a: Forced vital capacity (intubate if below about 20 mL/kg)
nodes.note: Measure it repeatedly. A negative inspiratory force weaker than -30 cm H2O is also a sign.

nodes.q: Which other complication explains his pulse swinging between 55 and 120 a minute?
nodes.a: Autonomic instability (arrhythmias and blood pressure swings)
nodes.note: Needs cardiac monitoring in intensive care.

nodes.q: Which cerebrospinal fluid result confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: High protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation)
nodes.note: Nerve conduction studies show slowed velocity or conduction block. Protein may be normal in the first week.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.note: Equal in benefit; steroids do not help. Add ventilatory support when needed.

nodes.q: Which variant adds ophthalmoplegia and ataxia to areflexia?
nodes.note: A descending pattern: eye muscles first. Anti-GQ1b antibodies are the marker.

nodes.q: His stress could suggest conversion disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Weakness that does not fit a nerve pattern; **normal reflexes, normal tone, and normal conduction studies**; Hoover sign
**Absent reflexes + sensory loss + falling forced vital capacity** after an infection

nodes.note: The trap: he has a real stressor, but stress can also precede Guillain-Barre syndrome, and absent reflexes are an objective sign.

nodes.q: His weakness could suggest poliomyelitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever and meningeal signs, then asymmetric flaccid weakness** with no sensory loss, from loss of anterior horn cells
**Symmetric ascending weakness + sensory loss + no fever**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited neurodegenerative disease of the striatum. The clincher: **chorea + progressive dementia + psychiatric change in a person with an affected parent, starting in mid-adult life**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern does the family history show?
nodes.note: Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the gene. Penetrance is complete once the repeat reaches 40 or more.

nodes.q: His healthy sister has a 3-year-old son. What is the chance that the boy will develop the disease?
nodes.note: She has a 50% chance of carrying the gene (their father was affected), and if she does, her son has a 50% chance of inheriting it: 0.5 x 0.5 = 25%. She is young enough that symptoms may not have started yet.

nodes.q: Which type of mutation causes the disease?

nodes.note: The repeat codes for a long run of glutamine in the huntingtin protein. Normal is under 27 repeats; 36 or more can cause disease, and 40 or more always do.

A biopsy of one lesion is stained and the cells are positive for cytokeratin. She has no fever, no immunodeficiency, and no skin or eye lesions of melanoma.
root.oneliner: 67F + 45 years of smoking + 3 weeks of morning headaches and left arm weakness + seizure + weight loss and chronic cough + multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction with swelling + cytokeratin-positive biopsy + no fever, no immunodeficiency, no melanoma
highlight: several ring-enhancing lesions at the junction of gray and white matter
no skin or eye lesions of melanoma

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Cancer cells spread to the brain from a tumor elsewhere. The clincher: **multiple enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction in an older smoker with a cytokeratin-positive biopsy**. Metastases are the most common brain tumors in adults.

nodes.q: Cytokeratin-positive cells arise from which cell type?
nodes.note: Cytokeratin is the intermediate filament of epithelial cells. Glial cells carry glial fibrillary acidic protein, neurons carry neurofilaments, muscle carries desmin and mesenchymal cells carry vimentin.

nodes.q: Which primary cancer most often spreads to the brain?
nodes.note: Then breast cancer, melanoma, kidney and colon cancer. Hemorrhagic metastases are typical of melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma and thyroid cancer.

nodes.q: Why do the lesions sit at the gray-white junction?
nodes.a: Tumor cells arrive in the blood and lodge where the arteries narrow at the gray-white junction
nodes.note: Spread is hematogenous.

nodes.q: Which type of swelling surrounds the lesions?
nodes.note: New tumor vessels lack a normal blood-brain barrier and leak fluid into the white matter. Cytotoxic edema, by contrast, is cell swelling from ischemia.

nodes.q: Which drug is given to reduce this swelling?
nodes.note: A glucocorticoid that tightens the leaky blood-brain barrier and reduces edema within hours to days.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment?
nodes.a: Radiation (stereotactic radiosurgery or whole-brain), with surgical removal of a solitary accessible lesion
nodes.note: Antiseizure drugs are given after a seizure, and the primary cancer is staged.

nodes.q: A ring-enhancing brain mass could be glioblastoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Single butterfly mass crossing the corpus callosum; pseudopalisading necrosis, glial fibrillary acidic protein positive**
**Multiple lesions at the gray-white junction; cytokeratin positive**

nodes.note: The trap: both are ring-enhancing masses with swelling.

nodes.q: Ring-enhancing lesions could suggest primary central nervous system lymphoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Usually **immunodeficiency (AIDS) with Epstein-Barr virus; periventricular ring-enhancing lesion; B cell markers**
**Immunocompetent smoker with epithelial cytokeratin-positive cells**

nodes.q: Her headaches and seizure could suggest a meningioma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Single dural-based mass with a dural tail and psammoma bodies**; slow growing
**Multiple intra-axial lesions with an epithelial cytokeratin-positive tumor**

root.stem: A 62-year-old man with a 15-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has had 5 months of burning pain in both feet that is worse at night in bed and eases in a hot bath; even the bedsheet touching his feet hurts. He drinks no alcohol and has no back pain. Pinprick and vibration sensation are reduced from just above the ankles down, and both ankle reflexes are decreased. Over the past month his left hand has become weak, with wasting of the muscles between the metacarpal bones and inability to spread his fingers, and he can no longer push his right foot down against resistance; strength is otherwise normal. He also feels dizzy on standing, and a painless ulcer has appeared under his left big toe. Capsaicin cream on his lower legs has eased the burning.
root.oneliner: 62M + 15 years of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes + burning feet, worse at night, better in hot bath + bedsheet pain + pinprick and vibration loss below the ankles + reduced ankle reflexes + strength otherwise normal + no alcohol, no back pain + left hand interosseous wasting, cannot spread fingers + right plantar flexion lost + dizzy on standing + painless toe ulcer + relief with capsaicin cream
highlight: even the bedsheet touching his feet hurts
Pinprick and vibration sensation are reduced from just above the ankles down
wasting of the muscles between the metacarpal bones
no longer push his right foot down

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Nerve damage from long-standing high blood glucose. The clincher: **burning feet with loss of pinprick and vibration from the ankles down in a long-standing diabetic**, with no alcohol use or back pain.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same disease: the most common form of diabetic nerve damage.

nodes.q: How will he describe the pain?
nodes.note: Typically worse at night in bed, when nothing distracts him, and eased by a hot bath. Light touch can hurt (allodynia). The burning comes from damaged small pain fibres; his separate weak muscles come from single-nerve infarcts, not from this stocking neuropathy.

nodes.q: Which change in the damaged pain fibres produces the burning?
nodes.a: Persistent activation of voltage-gated sodium channels in the nociceptors
nodes.note: Injured pain-fibre endings fire spontaneously because their sodium channels stay open. Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, lidocaine patch) quiet them.

nodes.q: Capsaicin cream eases the burning by depleting which neurotransmitter from the pain-fibre endings?
nodes.note: Capsaicin **activates** the vanilloid receptor (TRPV1) rather than blocking it: brief burning, then the substance P stores are exhausted and the fibres stop signalling.

nodes.q: Which enzyme turns the excess glucose into sorbitol inside nerve cells?
nodes.note: Sorbitol draws in water and depletes antioxidants. Narrowing of the small vessels that feed the nerve (vasa nervorum) adds ischemia.

nodes.q: Which pattern of sensory loss do you expect?
nodes.a: Stocking distribution, starting in the longest nerves
nodes.note: The longest axons fail first, so loss begins at the toes and climbs the legs; the hands ('glove') come later.

nodes.q: What does the lost pain sensation in the feet lead to?
nodes.note: Unnoticed pressure injuries, infection and sometimes amputation; a neuropathic (Charcot) joint can also develop.

nodes.q: What is the name for loss of several separate single nerves, like his hand and foot, appearing at random?
nodes.note: Vasa nervorum infarction knocks out one nerve at a time. The same mechanism causes oculomotor nerve palsy with a spared pupil in diabetics.

nodes.q: Which pair of nerves explains the wasted hand muscles and the lost plantar flexion?
nodes.note: Ulnar: interossei, so he cannot abduct the fingers. Tibial: plantar flexion of the foot. Median would waste the thenar muscles, radial gives wrist drop, common fibular gives foot drop.

nodes.q: Which other nerves does diabetes damage, causing the dizziness on standing?
nodes.note: Orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction and a neurogenic bladder.

nodes.q: Which bedside test screens for it?
nodes.a: 10-g monofilament test of the feet, with vibration testing
nodes.note: Done yearly, starting at diagnosis in type 2 diabetes.

nodes.q: Which measure slows progression of the nerve damage?
nodes.note: The benefit is strongest in type 1 diabetes.

nodes.q: Which first-line drug class for the pain blocks the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels?
nodes.note: Duloxetine and amitriptyline are alternatives; opioids are avoided.

nodes.q: His burning feet could suggest alcoholic neuropathy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Same painful stocking neuropathy, but **heavy alcohol use with thiamine and other vitamin deficiencies**; improves with abstinence and thiamine
**Long-standing high glucose with other diabetic complications and no alcohol**; autonomic and single-nerve involvement are common

nodes.note: The trap: both cause a painful, symmetric neuropathy of the feet.

nodes.q: His wasted hand could suggest carpal tunnel syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Median nerve: **thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction, night-time tingling of the thumb to ring finger**
Ulnar nerve: **interosseous wasting and inability to spread the fingers**, with a separate tibial nerve deficit in the foot

nodes.q: His lost plantar flexion could suggest an S1 radiculopathy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Back pain shooting down one leg in a dermatomal pattern**, one lost ankle reflex, positive straight-leg raise
**No back pain; both feet in a stocking pattern**, plus a tibial nerve deficit that fits a single nerve rather than a root

root.stem: A 48-year-old man who works in a delicatessen sliced through his right index finger with a meat slicer 6 months ago, and the finger was reattached by prompt surgery. The fingertip is still numb and the small hand muscles that move the finger have wasted. Tapping over the scar causes tingling that has slowly moved toward the fingertip, and the surgeon says sensation will come back gradually.
root.oneliner: 48M + deli worker + meat slicer cut through index finger, reattached + fingertip numb at 6 months + finger muscle wasting + tingling that advances from the scar
highlight: sliced through his right index finger
small hand muscles that move the finger have wasted
tingling that has slowly moved toward the fingertip

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A cut nerve: the part beyond the cut dies, then the axon regrows slowly. The clincher: **numbness and muscle wasting in the territory of a cut nerve, with tingling that advances 1 mm a day from the injury**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The most severe grade of nerve injury: axon and surrounding sheath are both cut.

nodes.q: What process destroys the axon and myelin beyond the cut?
nodes.note: Within days the distal axon and myelin break down, and macrophages clear the debris. The nerve cell body responds too.

nodes.q: Which structure left behind guides the regrowing axon?
nodes.a: Myelin sheath (the Schwann cell tube with its basal lamina)
nodes.note: Distal Schwann cells survive Wallerian degeneration, line up in columns inside the old basal lamina (bands of Bungner) and release growth factors, so the new axon follows the old path.

nodes.q: What happens in the nerve cell body in the dorsal root ganglion?
nodes.a: Chromatolysis: swelling with dispersal of Nissl substance
nodes.note: The cell body gears up protein synthesis to rebuild the axon; the nucleus moves to the edge.

nodes.q: What limits how fast sensation returns?
nodes.note: The cytoskeletal proteins for the new axon travel by slow transport, so regrowth runs at about 1 mm per day. The advancing tingling (Tinel sign) tracks the front.

nodes.q: Which peripheral glial cells, proliferating at the repair site, are most likely blocking reinnervation of his wasted muscles?
nodes.note: Axon sprouts from the proximal stump must cross the repair into the distal Schwann cell tubes. If the ends are gapped or misaligned, the sprouts grow in a disorganised tangle with proliferating Schwann cells and fibroblasts and never reach the muscle: a **traumatic (amputation) neuroma**, a tender lump at the scar. Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia are central nervous system cells, and satellite cells surround ganglion cell bodies (or repair muscle), so none of them sits in the path of a finger nerve.

nodes.q: Meanwhile, what happens to the denervated muscle fibres?
nodes.note: If reinnervation never comes, fat and fibrous tissue replace the muscle.

nodes.q: If surviving nerve branches do reinnervate the muscle, which pattern appears on biopsy?
nodes.note: Sprouting axons convert the fibres they take over to their own type, so fibres of one type cluster together instead of the normal checkerboard mix.

nodes.q: Which repair is done for a clean cut seen early?
nodes.note: A gap is bridged with a nerve graft; long delay allows the distal sheath and muscle to degenerate.

nodes.q: His numbness could suggest neurapraxia, as after a stretch injury. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Focal conduction block with the axon intact and no Wallerian degeneration**; recovers fully in days to weeks
**Axon and sheath cut, with Wallerian degeneration**; needs surgery and regrowth at about 1 mm a day

nodes.note: The trap: both give numbness after trauma.

nodes.q: A crush injury could also cause Wallerian degeneration. How do you tell it from a cut?

split.note: **Axon destroyed but the endoneurial tubes stay intact**, so axons regrow along them and surgery is usually not needed
**Tubes severed as well**, so regrowth is misdirected without surgical repair

nodes.q: A cut axon in the spinal cord might be expected to regrow the same way. How do you tell the two apart?

split.note: **Oligodendrocytes myelinate and astrocytes form a glial scar**; no Schwann cell tube, so almost no regrowth
**Schwann cells form guiding tubes and release growth factors**, so axons can regrow

nodes.q: Slowed conduction without an axon cut could suggest a demyelinating neuropathy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Myelin attacked but axons intact**; conduction slows and recovery is by remyelination, with no Wallerian degeneration
**Axon severed, with Wallerian degeneration beyond the cut** and a single injured nerve

root.stem: A 34-year-old man who smokes a pack a day comes in because of a 2-week history of severe stabbing pain behind his left eye that wakes him from sleep each night, about 90 minutes after he lies down. The pain builds over about 5 minutes and lasts 45 minutes, and during it he cannot lie still and paces the room. During each attack the left eye is red and waters, the left nostril runs and feels blocked, and the left eyelid droops slightly. A beer in the evening has triggered attacks during this period. He had a similar 2-month period last year, followed by months without headache. He has no fever or neck stiffness, no sneezing or itching, no scalp tenderness or jaw pain on chewing, and no vomiting or light sensitivity. Vital signs are normal, the optic discs are sharp, and the neurologic examination is normal.
root.oneliner: 34M + smoker + nightly stabbing pain behind left eye, 45 min + restless, paces + red watering eye, blocked runny nostril, mild ptosis + beer triggers + same pattern last year then remission + no fever or neck stiffness, no sneezing, no scalp tenderness, no nausea or photophobia + normal exam and fundi
highlight: severe stabbing pain behind his left eye
wakes him from sleep each night
no scalp tenderness or jaw pain on chewing

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A rare primary headache of young men. The clincher: **short (15 to 180 minutes) one-sided pain around the eye with same-side tearing, red eye and runny nose, recurring daily in bouts**.

nodes.q: Why is it called a cluster headache?
nodes.a: Attacks come daily for weeks to months, then stop for months to years
nodes.note: Cluster periods often return in the same season. Attacks often start at night, a few hours into sleep.

nodes.q: Which common drink triggers an attack during a cluster period but not during remission?
nodes.note: Outside a cluster period alcohol does nothing. This is not simply vasodilation, and it is advised to avoid alcohol during bouts.

nodes.q: Which brain region is thought to drive the clock-like attacks?
nodes.note: Overactive hypothalamic grey matter (circadian control) triggers the trigeminal pain pathway.

nodes.q: What causes the red, watering eye and blocked, runny nostril on the painful side?
nodes.a: Overactivity of the parasympathetic reflex through the trigeminal and facial nerves
nodes.note: The trigeminal-autonomic reflex fires with the pain.

nodes.q: What causes the drooping eyelid during an attack?
nodes.note: Swelling of the carotid wall near the cavernous sinus is thought to compress sympathetic fibres; ptosis and a small pupil on the same side.

nodes.q: Which imaging is advised at first presentation?
nodes.a: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain
nodes.note: It rules out a pituitary or vascular lesion that can mimic it.

nodes.q: Which non-drug treatment aborts an attack?
nodes.a: 100% oxygen by face mask at 12 to 15 L/min
nodes.note: Given for about 15 minutes.

nodes.q: Which injected drug also aborts an attack within minutes?
nodes.note: A serotonin 5-HT1B/1D agonist that constricts cranial vessels; avoid in coronary artery disease.

nodes.q: Which calcium channel blocker is first-line to prevent attacks during a cluster period?
nodes.note: Check an electrocardiogram for PR prolongation; a short course of prednisone bridges the gap.

nodes.q: His headache could suggest migraine. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Lasts **4 to 72 hours, throbbing, with nausea and light sensitivity; the patient lies still in the dark**; more often women
Lasts **15 to 180 minutes with tearing, red eye and blocked nostril; the patient paces**; more often men

nodes.note: The trap: both are one-sided headaches that recur.

nodes.q: His headache could suggest tension-type headache. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dull, pressing band around both sides of the head, mild, no autonomic signs**; lasts hours
**Severe one-sided stabbing pain with same-side eye and nose signs**

nodes.q: His eye pain could suggest temporal arteritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Over 50, **scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, high erythrocyte sedimentation rate**, risk of sudden vision loss; pain is persistent
Young man, **attacks last under 3 hours with restlessness and autonomic signs; none of the jaw or scalp findings**

nodes.q: His sudden pain could suggest subarachnoid hemorrhage. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Thunderclap pain peaking in seconds, worst headache of life, neck stiffness**; a single event
**Builds over minutes and repeats in the same pattern for years** with a normal exam

nodes.q: His red, watering eye and blocked nostril could suggest allergic rhinitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sneezing, itching, both sides, seasonal triggers, little pain**
**Severe one-sided eye pain with the same-side eye and nose signs** and no sneezing or itching

nodes.q: His new headaches could suggest an intracranial mass. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Progressive headaches, worse on waking, with vomiting, papilledema or focal deficits**
**Episodic attacks with long pain-free remissions, sharp optic discs and a normal neurologic exam**

nodes.q: His pain could suggest acute meningitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, neck stiffness and light sensitivity** in a single acute illness
**No fever or neck stiffness; the same brief attacks return year after year**

nodes.q: His headache could suggest idiopathic intracranial hypertension. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Overweight young woman, daily pressure headache with papilledema and pulsatile tinnitus**
**Man with brief one-sided attacks and sharp optic discs**
