root.stem: A 36-year-old woman with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection is brought in after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She has had 2 months of daily headaches, her left arm is weak, and her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 22/mm3. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a single 3-cm enhancing mass in the right cerebral hemisphere next to the lateral ventricle with mild surrounding edema. Her Toxoplasma gondii IgG is positive and she has taken pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine for 2 weeks, but the mass has grown and she has had three more seizures. She has no fever, no neck stiffness and no known cancer elsewhere. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the cerebrospinal fluid detects Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA.
root.oneliner: 36F + HIV with CD4 22 + seizure, headaches, left arm weakness + single 3-cm enhancing mass beside the lateral ventricle + Toxoplasma IgG positive + mass grew after 2 weeks of pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine + no fever, no known primary cancer + EBV DNA in cerebrospinal fluid

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A lymphoma that starts in the brain. The clincher: **a single enhancing brain mass in advanced HIV that keeps growing despite 2 weeks of toxoplasmosis treatment, with EBV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid**.

nodes.q: Which type of cancer is it?
nodes.a: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, usually diffuse large B-cell
nodes.note: Nearly all AIDS-related cases are B-cell tumors.

nodes.q: The virus found in her cerebrospinal fluid drives this tumor. Which receptor does it use to enter B cells?
nodes.note: Epstein-Barr virus binds CD21 through its gp350 envelope protein and keeps the B cells it infects alive. In AIDS, EBV DNA by PCR in the cerebrospinal fluid, with a typical scan, strongly supports the diagnosis.

nodes.q: Why does the tumor appear at this stage of HIV?
nodes.a: T-cell control of EBV-infected B cells is lost at very low CD4 counts
nodes.note: It usually appears when the CD4 count falls below about 50/mm3.

nodes.q: If the cerebrospinal fluid test is negative or not possible, what is the next step after the mass keeps growing on antitoxoplasma treatment?
nodes.note: Treatment with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine for 10 to 14 days is the usual first trial for a mass with positive Toxoplasma IgG.

nodes.q: Why should corticosteroids be held before biopsy if possible?
nodes.a: They can shrink the lymphoma and make the tissue non-diagnostic
nodes.note: Lymphoma cells are killed by steroids and can vanish ('ghost tumor').

nodes.q: Which folate-antagonist chemotherapy given in high dose is the backbone of treatment?
nodes.note: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and crosses the blood-brain barrier at high dose; given with leucovorin rescue plus antiretroviral therapy.

nodes.q: Her positive Toxoplasma IgG could suggest cerebral toxoplasmosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Multiple ring-enhancing lesions, often in the basal ganglia, that shrink within 2 weeks of pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine**
**Single mass beside the ventricle that grows despite treatment, with EBV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid**

nodes.note: The trap: IgG is positive in many people with HIV and does not prove active disease.

nodes.q: Her seizure and mass could suggest a bacterial abscess. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever and a source (endocarditis, sinusitis, dental)**; ring enhancement with a bright center on diffusion imaging
**No fever; no source; EBV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid**

nodes.q: Her single enhancing mass could suggest glioblastoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Older adult, **irregular ring-enhancing mass crossing the corpus callosum ('butterfly') with necrosis and pseudopalisading**; not tied to HIV
**Advanced HIV, mass beside the ventricle, EBV DNA in the fluid**

nodes.q: Her mass could suggest metastatic disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Several lesions at the gray-white junction with a known lung, breast or melanoma primary**
**Single lesion and no known cancer elsewhere**

nodes.q: Her weakness could suggest progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **JC virus: multifocal non-enhancing white-matter lesions with no mass effect**
**Enhancing mass with edema and EBV DNA**

root.stem: A 29-year-old man has had difficulty seeing in dim light since his teens and, over the last two years, has been bumping into objects at his sides. His hearing is normal and he has no other illnesses. Dilated eye examination shows dark, branching bone-spicule pigment in the mid-periphery of both retinas, thin retinal arteries and a pale optic disc, with the macula spared. His father had the same night vision problem and passed it on to him, and his father's sister and her daughter are affected as well. An electroretinogram shows markedly reduced rod responses.
root.oneliner: 29M + night blindness since teens + recent tunnel vision + normal hearing + bone-spicule pigment, thin arteries, pale disc + affected father, aunt and cousin + reduced rod electroretinogram
highlight: bumping into objects at his sides
His father had the same night vision problem and passed it on to him
father's sister and her daughter are affected

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited degeneration of the retina. The clincher: **night blindness followed by tunnel vision, with bone-spicule pigment and a reduced rod electroretinogram**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Rods fail first, then cones.

nodes.q: Which symptom appears first?
nodes.note: Rods, which work in dim light, sit mostly in the periphery of the retina and die first.

nodes.q: What happens to the visual field later?
nodes.note: The peripheral field narrows; central vision is lost late, so people read well but bump into things.

nodes.q: What forms the dark bone-spicule pigment?
nodes.a: Pigment-laden cells migrating from the retinal pigment epithelium into the retina around the vessels
nodes.note: They collect around the retinal vessels in the mid-periphery as rods die.

nodes.q: His father passed the disease to him. Which mode of inheritance does this father-to-son transmission rule out?
nodes.a: X-linked inheritance (the X-linked recessive form of retinitis pigmentosa)
nodes.note: A son receives his father's Y, not his X. Autosomal dominant (as here, with affected people in each generation) and autosomal recessive both remain possible, so the rest of the pedigree tells them apart.

nodes.q: Several different genes can cause identical disease. What is this called?
nodes.note: Rhodopsin gene mutations are the most common autosomal dominant cause.

nodes.q: Which test shows loss of rod function even before the fundus looks abnormal?
nodes.note: It measures the electrical response of the retina to light and is reduced or absent.

nodes.q: Which lens opacity often develops?
nodes.note: Cystoid macular edema can also reduce central vision.

nodes.q: Which gene therapy is approved for retinal dystrophy caused by mutations in both copies of the retinal pigment epithelium 65-kDa protein (RPE65) gene?
nodes.note: An adeno-associated virus vector that delivers a working RPE65 gene by subretinal injection; the patient needs enough surviving retinal cells. RPE65 regenerates 11-cis-retinal for the visual cycle. It does not help his dominant form, which is usually a rhodopsin mutation; for him, care is genetic counseling, low-vision aids and cataract surgery as needed.

nodes.q: His eye findings could suggest Usher syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Autosomal recessive; **retinitis pigmentosa together with sensorineural hearing loss, often present from birth**
**Normal hearing**; here a dominant pedigree with male-to-male transmission

nodes.note: The trap: Usher syndrome is the most common cause of combined deafness and blindness and includes retinitis pigmentosa.

nodes.q: Poor vision from retinal degeneration could suggest Leber congenital amaurosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Severe vision loss, roving eyes and a flat electroretinogram from infancy**; RPE65 is one of its genes, the main target of the gene therapy
**Night blindness appearing in the teens and slowly narrowing fields**

nodes.q: His night blindness could suggest vitamin A deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fat malabsorption or poor diet, dry eyes with Bitot spots**, normal retinal pigment; reversible with vitamin A
**Bone-spicule pigment and an affected family; no response to vitamin A**

nodes.q: His pigmentary retinopathy could suggest abetalipoproteinemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Childhood fat malabsorption, acanthocytes on the smear and ataxia from vitamin E deficiency**; very low cholesterol; recessive
**Eye disease alone in a healthy adult with a dominant pedigree**

root.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after he bit off the tip of his tongue and then walked for two days on a fractured left ankle without complaining. He has never cried with injections, has several healed burns on his fingers from touching a hot stove, and has a swollen, deformed right knee. He sweats normally and has never had unexplained high fevers, and his intelligence is normal. Light touch, vibration and position sense are intact, and deep tendon reflexes are normal. His parents are healthy first cousins.
root.oneliner: 4M + bit off tongue tip + walked on a fracture for 2 days + no crying with injections + burns on fingers + deformed right knee + normal sweating, no fevers + normal intelligence + normal touch, vibration, position + reflexes + parents first cousins
highlight: bit off the tip of his tongue
walked for two days on a fractured left ankle
Light touch, vibration and position sense are intact

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A rare inherited loss of pain perception. The clincher: **no pain from injuries with normal touch, vibration, position sense, sweating and intelligence**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same condition.

nodes.q: Which neurons carry the pain sensation that is lost?
nodes.a: Small-diameter neurons of the dorsal root ganglia
nodes.note: Their thin A-delta and C fibres carry pain and temperature. Large-diameter neurons carry touch, vibration and position, which stay intact.

nodes.q: From which embryonic tissue do these neurons arise?
nodes.note: The dorsal root ganglia neurons, Schwann cells and postganglionic autonomic neurons are all neural crest derivatives.

nodes.q: Which channel is non-functional in many families?
nodes.note: Loss-of-function mutations, inherited in an autosomal recessive way (as with the cousin parents), mean pain fibres cannot fire. Gain-of-function mutations cause the opposite: erythromelalgia.

nodes.q: What is the swollen, deformed knee?
nodes.note: Repeated unnoticed injuries destroy the joint; fractures and burns are missed as well.

nodes.q: What is the main lifelong management?
nodes.a: Preventing injuries with frequent skin, joint and eye inspections
nodes.note: Also protective gear for the mouth and genetic counseling; no drug restores pain sensation.

nodes.q: His lack of pain could suggest congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.a: Congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis
split.note: **No sweating, recurrent high fevers and heat stroke, intellectual disability**; NTRK1 (nerve growth factor receptor) mutation; loses sympathetic postganglionic neurons as well
**Normal sweating and intelligence**; sodium channel defect

nodes.note: The trap: both show painless injuries and self-mutilation.

nodes.q: His painless burns could suggest leprosy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Acquired from **Mycobacterium leprae** in an endemic area; **numb pale skin patches and thickened nerves**
**Present from birth with no skin patches or nerve thickening**

nodes.q: His bitten tongue could suggest Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

His serum sodium is 104 mEq/L and his potassium is 2.8 mEq/L, and he has no eye movement problems or unsteady gait. He has no fever or neck stiffness, and his sensation is intact.

slurred speech, difficulty swallowing and weakness of all four limbs
look up and down and blink

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Loss of myelin after a too-fast rise in serum sodium. The clincher: **dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis 2 to 6 days after rapid sodium correction**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The name for the pontine form of the same process.

nodes.q: What set it off?
nodes.note: Here sodium rose 20 mEq/L in 14 hours.

nodes.q: What is the maximum safe rise in serum sodium over 24 hours for a high-risk patient like him?
nodes.note: High risk: sodium of 120 or less, alcohol use, hypokalemia, malnutrition or liver disease. In others the limit is 10 to 12 mEq/L. Check sodium every 2 to 4 hours.

nodes.q: Which electrolyte abnormality, besides the low sodium, raises his risk?
nodes.note: Alcoholism, malnutrition and liver disease also raise the risk.

nodes.q: Which brain cells are destroyed?
nodes.note: Chronically swollen brain cells lost osmolytes to adapt; a fast sodium rise shrinks them and the myelin-making oligodendrocytes die.

nodes.q: Where is the lesion?
nodes.a: Central basis pontis (pons) of the brainstem
nodes.note: Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres cross the pons, causing quadriparesis, dysarthria and dysphagia.

nodes.q: When only vertical eye movements and blinking are left, what is it called?
nodes.note: The ventral pons is destroyed but the midbrain, which moves the eyes vertically, is spared. Awareness is intact.

nodes.q: What is the typical course?
nodes.a: Initial improvement, then new neurologic deficits 2 to 6 days later
nodes.note: Delayed onset helps separate it from the original encephalopathy.

nodes.q: Where else can the lesions occur, causing parkinsonism or dystonia?
nodes.a: Extrapontine sites such as the basal ganglia
nodes.note: Seen in some patients together with the pontine lesion.

nodes.q: Which test shows the lesion, though it may need 1 to 2 weeks to appear?
nodes.a: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
nodes.note: Bright signal in the central pons on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images.

nodes.q: What is the rescue if sodium rose too fast?
nodes.a: Re-lower the sodium with dextrose 5% in water plus desmopressin
nodes.note: Desmopressin (a vasopressin analogue) stops free water loss while the sodium is brought back.

nodes.q: His confusion and alcohol use could suggest Wernicke encephalopathy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Confusion with ophthalmoplegia and ataxia present on admission**; mammillary bodies and medial thalamus; thiamine deficiency
**Dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis after fast sodium correction**, with eye movements intact

nodes.note: The trap: both occur in alcoholic patients; Wernicke affects the medial diencephalon, not the pons.

nodes.q: His brainstem signs could suggest a basilar artery stroke. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden onset with vascular risk factors**; infarct on diffusion imaging
**Delayed onset after a fast sodium rise** with demyelination and no infarct

nodes.q: His weakness of all four limbs could suggest Guillain-Barre syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Ascending weakness with lost reflexes and sensory symptoms**, often after an infection; peripheral nerve
**Brisk reflexes, dysarthria and dysphagia, with intact sensation**; brainstem

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited tumor syndrome. The clincher: **hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum, retina and spinal cord, with kidney cancer in the family**.

nodes.q: Which tumor suppressor gene is lost?
nodes.note: Autosomal dominant; tumors arise after the second hit (Knudson two-hit hypothesis).

nodes.q: What accumulates in the cells because the lost gene can no longer mark it for degradation?
nodes.note: The VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin ligase that tags hypoxia-inducible factor for destruction. Without it, the factor drives vascular endothelial growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor and erythropoietin, so tumors are very vascular and the blood count rises.

nodes.q: Why is his hemoglobin high?

nodes.note: Erythropoietin from a hemangioblastoma or kidney tumor causes secondary polycythemia.

nodes.q: What is the cerebellar tumor?

nodes.q: Which kidney neoplasm is he at increased risk for?
nodes.note: Often bilateral and multiple, and it appears early, like his father's cancer at 44.

nodes.q: Which adrenal tumor explains the episodes of sweating, palpitations and severe hypertension?
nodes.note: Check plasma metanephrines.

nodes.q: Which other abdominal organ develops cysts and neuroendocrine tumors in this disease?

nodes.q: What surveillance is done for known carriers?
nodes.a: Yearly eye examinations from infancy and plasma metanephrines from early childhood, plus regular magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, spine and abdomen from adolescence
nodes.note: The aim is to find hemangioblastomas, kidney tumors and pheochromocytomas while small.

nodes.q: Which oral drug, blocking the transcription factor that builds up in his cells, is used for his tumors?
nodes.note: Belzutifan blocks hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha. It is approved for VHL-related renal cell carcinoma, central nervous system hemangioblastomas and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors that do not need surgery at once. Because it lowers erythropoietin, its main side effect is anemia; hypoxia also occurs.

nodes.q: His kidney risk could suggest tuberous sclerosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Seizures, hypomelanotic skin patches, facial angiofibromas, cardiac rhabdomyomas**; kidney angiomyolipomas and subependymal nodules
**Hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum, retina and spinal cord; clear cell renal carcinoma**

nodes.note: The trap: both involve brain and kidney tumors.

nodes.q: His brain tumors could suggest neurofibromatosis type 2. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, juvenile cataracts**
**Cerebellar and cord hemangioblastomas with a retinal capillary mass**

nodes.q: His family kidney tumor could suggest Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Skin fibrofolliculomas, lung cysts with spontaneous pneumothorax**; oncocytoma and chromophobe kidney tumors
**Clear cell renal carcinoma with cerebellar hemangioblastomas**

split.note: **Child under 5 with a large flank mass**; WT1 deletion with aniridia in WAGR syndrome
**Adult-onset clear cell carcinoma in a patient with hemangioblastomas**

She has past-pointing on finger-nose testing and a broad-based gait. Her legs are stiff with brisk reflexes and sustained clonus, and painful muscle cramps disturb her sleep. blurs further after a hot shower
does not move past the midline
adducts normally when she focuses on a near object
stiff with brisk reflexes and sustained clonus

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, most often in young women. The clincher: **neurologic attacks separated in time and in space (optic nerve, brainstem, cerebellum) with white-matter plaques of different ages on MRI**.

nodes.q: Which pattern of attacks makes the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Episodes months apart, each affecting a different part of the central nervous system (dissemination in time and in space)
nodes.note: Her right-eye episodes a year apart, plus brainstem and cerebellar signs now, fit this. Enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on one scan also prove lesions of different ages. Most patients start with a relapsing-remitting course.

nodes.q: What is the immune mechanism?
nodes.a: CD4+ T helper cells (Th1 and Th17) activated against myelin proteins such as myelin basic protein
nodes.note: Activated T cells and macrophages attack central myelin. It is not an antibody against axons, a CD8+ T-cell attack on astrocytes, immune-complex deposition or a vasculitis. Risk rises with distance from the equator (low vitamin D) and after Epstein-Barr virus infection.

nodes.q: Which cells make the myelin that is lost?
nodes.note: One oligodendrocyte myelinates several central axons. Peripheral myelin comes from Schwann cells, so peripheral nerves are spared.

nodes.q: Which human leukocyte antigen (HLA) type raises the risk of this disease?
nodes.note: An HLA class II allele, which fits a CD4+ T-cell disease. Compare HLA-DR3 and DR4 in type 1 diabetes, and HLA-B27 in the spondyloarthritides.

nodes.q: What does a plaque show under the microscope?
nodes.a: Sharply bordered loss of myelin with relatively preserved axons, later replaced by astrocyte scarring (gliosis)
nodes.note: Active plaques hold T cells and lipid-laden macrophages around small veins. Plaques favour the white matter around the lateral ventricles (on sagittal MRI they point away from the ventricles as 'Dawson fingers'), the optic nerves, brainstem, cerebellum and spinal cord. Axons are lost over time, which drives permanent disability.

nodes.q: Which cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) finding supports the diagnosis?
nodes.note: IgG made inside the central nervous system shows as several bands in the cerebrospinal fluid that are absent from serum. The protein and white cell count are only mildly raised. Magnetic resonance imaging of brain and spinal cord with gadolinium remains the most sensitive test for the plaques.

nodes.q: Her vision blurs further after a hot shower. What is this called?
nodes.note: Heat slows and blocks conduction along demyelinated axons, so old symptoms return briefly; they recover on cooling. It is not a new attack.

nodes.q: Which structure explains her blurred vision in the right eye?
nodes.note: Often the first attack: pain on moving the eye and loss of central vision. The disc often looks normal at first because the inflammation lies behind the eye (retrobulbar).

nodes.q: On the swinging-flashlight test both pupils dilate when the light moves to her right eye. What is this sign called?
nodes.a: Relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil)
nodes.note: Light in the left eye reaches the brainstem and constricts both pupils, so both efferent (oculomotor) pathways and both Edinger-Westphal nuclei work. Light in the right eye is poorly conducted by the damaged right optic nerve, so both pupils dilate. The pupils stay equal at rest.

nodes.q: Why is her right optic disc pale?
nodes.a: Optic atrophy: loss of the optic nerve axons after the earlier attack

nodes.q: Her right eye fails to adduct on left gaze but adducts on convergence. What is this eye movement disorder?
nodes.note: The eye that fails to adduct is on the side of the lesion. The opposite eye abducts, often with jerking nystagmus.

nodes.q: Which structure is damaged?
nodes.a: The right medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the brainstem
nodes.note: This heavily myelinated tract links the abducens nucleus on one side with the oculomotor nucleus (medial rectus) on the other for conjugate gaze. Convergence uses a separate pathway, so it is spared. Bilateral INO in a young adult is nearly diagnostic of multiple sclerosis.

nodes.q: Which part of the nervous system explains her past-pointing and broad-based gait?
nodes.a: The cerebellum (plaques in the cerebellar white matter)
nodes.note: Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia on the same side as the lesion. Charcot's classic triad in this disease is scanning speech, intention tremor and nystagmus.

nodes.q: Which neurons are damaged to cause stiff legs, brisk reflexes and clonus?
nodes.note: Loss of descending inhibition gives spasticity, hyperreflexia and clonus.

nodes.q: Which first-line oral antispasticity drug, also given intrathecally by an implanted pump, eases her stiffness and cramps?
nodes.note: Alternatives: tizanidine (an alpha-2 agonist in the spinal cord) and dantrolene (acts in muscle).

nodes.q: Which receptor does baclofen stimulate?
nodes.a: The gamma-aminobutyric acid type B (GABA-B) receptor
nodes.note: A Gi-coupled receptor: it opens potassium channels and lowers calcium entry, so less excitatory transmitter is released onto spinal motor neurons. Stopping it abruptly can cause seizures. Dantrolene instead blocks the ryanodine receptor in muscle.

nodes.q: Which drug shortens an acute attack?
nodes.note: It speeds recovery but does not change long-term disability. Plasmapheresis is used if steroids fail.

nodes.q: Which drug group lowers the number of future relapses?
nodes.note: Started early to reduce relapses and new MRI lesions; they do not repair damage already done.

nodes.q: Which injected cytokine was the first disease-modifying drug for this disease?
nodes.note: It shifts the immune response away from inflammatory T-cell activity. Adverse effects: flu-like symptoms after injections, depression, raised liver enzymes and low blood counts. Glatiramer acetate is another older injected choice.

nodes.q: Which monoclonal antibody blocks alpha-4 integrin so that lymphocytes cannot cross into the brain?
nodes.note: Highly effective for relapses. Ocrelizumab (anti-CD20, depletes B cells) is another antibody used in this disease.

nodes.q: Which brain infection is its feared adverse effect?
nodes.note: Reactivation of the JC virus destroys oligodendrocytes and causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, often fatal. Check anti-JC virus antibodies before and during treatment.

nodes.q: Her pupil findings could suggest an oculomotor nerve lesion. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Large pupil that does not constrict to light in either eye, with ptosis and the eye down and out**; the other pupil still constricts to light shone in the affected eye
**Both pupils equal at rest; light swung to the affected eye makes both dilate (afferent defect)**; no ptosis

nodes.note: The trap: both give an abnormal pupil response, but one is a lost output to the pupil and the other a lost input from the eye.

nodes.q: Her optic neuritis could suggest neuromyelitis optica (NMO). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Aquaporin-4 antibodies + severe optic neuritis, often both eyes, with a spinal cord lesion over 3 or more vertebral segments**; brain MRI usually normal
**Periventricular and cerebellar plaques + internuclear ophthalmoplegia + oligoclonal bands**; spinal lesions are short

nodes.q: Multifocal white-matter lesions could suggest acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Child, 1 to 3 weeks after a viral infection or vaccine, with fever and confusion in a single attack**
**Young adult with separate attacks a year apart and no fever or confusion**

long hours reading and working on a computer

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A recurrent primary headache disorder. The clincher: **unilateral throbbing headache with nausea and light sensitivity, preceded by a spreading visual aura, with a normal neurologic examination**.

nodes.q: Which symptom just before the headache is the strongest clue?
nodes.a: A visual aura of slowly enlarging flashing arcs lasting 5 to 60 minutes
nodes.note: The aura is fully reversible and builds up gradually, unlike the sudden onset of a transient ischemic attack.

nodes.q: Which brain event causes the aura?
nodes.a: Cortical spreading depression, a slow wave of depolarization across the occipital cortex
nodes.note: The wave moves about 3 mm per minute, matching the slowly enlarging lights.

nodes.q: Which peptide released from trigeminal nerve endings dilates meningeal vessels and drives the pain?
nodes.note: This is the trigeminovascular theory. Antibodies against CGRP or its receptor are used for prevention.

nodes.q: Which hormone change commonly triggers attacks in women?
nodes.note: Attacks often come just before menses and can return or worsen with changes in estrogen, as when she took the pill.

nodes.q: She wants the most effective contraception that contains no hormones. Which should the physician recommend?
nodes.note: Failure rate is below 1 percent. Estrogen-containing contraceptives are avoided in migraine with aura because they add to the risk of ischemic stroke.

nodes.q: She asks for a brain scan to rule out a tumor. Which response is best?
nodes.a: Ask what she thinks is causing her headaches
nodes.note: Exploring her worry first keeps her engaged and lets the physician address it; then explain that her typical history and normal examination make a scan unnecessary. Imaging is kept for red flags: thunderclap onset, focal deficits, papilledema, or a new headache after age 50.

nodes.q: Which drug group aborts an attack?
nodes.note: Best taken early in the headache phase. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs help mild attacks; antiemetics such as metoclopramide treat the nausea.

nodes.q: Which receptors do triptans stimulate?
nodes.note: They constrict dilated cranial vessels and block the release of CGRP and other peptides from trigeminal endings.

nodes.q: In which patients are triptans unsafe because they constrict arteries?
nodes.a: Those with coronary artery disease or prior stroke
nodes.note: Also avoided in Prinzmetal angina and uncontrolled hypertension.

nodes.q: If her attacks became frequent, which nonselective beta blocker is the classic preventive drug?
nodes.note: Topiramate, amitriptyline and antibodies against calcitonin gene-related peptide are alternatives.

nodes.q: Her computer work and job stress could suggest tension-type headache. How do you tell them apart?

**Unilateral throbbing pain with nausea, light sensitivity, a visual aura and exhaustion afterward**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Paroxysmal pain in the territory of the trigeminal nerve, usually after age 50 and more often in women. The clincher: **brief electric-shock pains in the cheek or jaw set off by light touch, chewing or brushing teeth, with a normal examination**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which divisions of the trigeminal nerve usually carry the pain?
nodes.note: They supply the cheek, upper lip, lower jaw and teeth; the maxillary division leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum and the mandibular through the foramen ovale. The ophthalmic division is rarely involved.

nodes.q: What is the most common cause?
nodes.a: Compression of the trigeminal root by a looping artery (usually the superior cerebellar artery) near the brainstem
nodes.note: The pulsing vessel focally strips the myelin of the root. Light-touch fibres then excite pain fibres across the damaged sheath, so a harmless touch triggers a stab.

nodes.q: Suppose a 30-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis had the same shooting pains. Where would the responsible plaque most likely be?
nodes.a: The pons (where the trigeminal root enters the brainstem)
nodes.note: Suspect a plaque when the pain begins before age 40 or affects both sides. In this 54-year-old with no other neurologic history, compression by a vessel is far more likely than a plaque.

nodes.q: Which test is done to look for the cause?
nodes.a: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with magnetic resonance angiography
nodes.note: It shows a compressing vessel, a plaque, or a tumor at the root.

nodes.q: Which drug is first-line?
nodes.note: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and prefers rapidly firing neurons. Adverse effects: hyponatremia (from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), aplastic anemia, liver injury, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome in carriers of HLA-B*15:02; it also induces cytochrome P450 enzymes.

nodes.q: Which operation is offered when drugs fail?

nodes.note: Percutaneous rhizotomy or gamma-knife radiosurgery are other options.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?

nodes.q: Which part of the developing neural tube is malformed?
nodes.note: The metencephalon is the upper part of the hindbrain (rhombencephalon) and gives rise to the cerebellum and the pons; the myelencephalon forms the medulla. The mesencephalon forms the midbrain, the diencephalon the thalamus, and the telencephalon the cerebral hemispheres.

nodes.q: Which complication explains his big head and tense fontanelle?
nodes.note: The outlets of the fourth ventricle (foramina of Luschka and Magendie) fail to open, so cerebrospinal fluid builds up in the cyst and the lateral ventricles. This is a non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus.

nodes.q: Which eye sign shows the raised pressure?
nodes.note: Pressure on the dorsal midbrain (tectum) paralyses upward gaze, as in Parinaud syndrome, so the eyes sink and the sclera shows above the iris.

nodes.q: How is the hydrocephalus treated?
nodes.a: A cerebrospinal fluid shunt (ventriculoperitoneal or cystoperitoneal)
nodes.note: Done early to protect the developing brain.

nodes.q: Which other brain malformation is often found with it?
nodes.note: Heart defects and other midline anomalies can also occur, so a full screen is needed.

nodes.q: A big head and hydrocephalus in an infant could suggest Chiari type II malformation. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small posterior fossa with the vermis and medulla pulled down through the foramen magnum, plus a lumbosacral myelomeningocele**
**Large posterior fossa with a midline cyst and absent vermis; no myelomeningocele**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause hydrocephalus and involve the posterior fossa.

nodes.q: A midline brain malformation could suggest holoprosencephaly. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Single fused ventricle and incomplete forebrain division with midline facial defects (cleft lip, close-set eyes)**
**Forebrain divided normally; the defect is in the cerebellum and posterior fossa**

nodes.q: His enlarged lateral ventricles could suggest isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Absent callosal fibres with widely separated, parallel lateral ventricles**; posterior fossa and vermis normal, head size usually normal
**Posterior fossa cyst with absent vermis**

nodes.q: Large ventricles could suggest hydrocephalus ex vacuo. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Ventricles enlarged because brain tissue has shrunk; head size normal or small and fontanelle soft**
**Enlarging head with a tense fontanelle from obstructed flow, plus a posterior fossa cyst**

nodes.q: A brain anomaly found on a well-child visit could raise the question of Down syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Flat facial profile, upslanting eyes, low tone and a single palmar crease (trisomy 21)**; head circumference usually small, no posterior fossa cyst
**Rapidly enlarging head with a posterior fossa cyst on imaging**

root.stem: A 62-year-old man has had intermittent severe pain in his left foot for 2 months, beginning soon after his left leg was amputated below the knee. The pain is throbbing, aching and shooting, and each episode lasts several seconds to a few minutes. He feels it in the toes and sole of the foot that is no longer there. It is worse when he is anxious or when the temperature changes, and it does not ease when he changes position. The stump has healed and is not tender or red, and he has no fever or back pain.
root.oneliner: 62M + severe throbbing, aching, shooting pain in the missing left foot for 2 months after below-knee amputation + episodes of seconds to minutes + worse with anxiety and temperature change + not relieved by position + healed non-tender stump, no fever, no back pain
highlight: toes and sole of the foot that is no longer there
several seconds to a few minutes
worse when he is anxious or when the temperature changes
does not ease when he changes position
healed and is not tender or red

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Pain felt in a body part that has been removed. The clincher: **throbbing, shooting pain localized to the missing limb, beginning soon after amputation and worse with anxiety or temperature change**.

nodes.q: What is the painless version called?
nodes.note: Most amputees feel the missing limb (tingling, position, movement) without pain.

nodes.q: What change in the brain is thought to underlie it?
nodes.a: Cortical reorganization: neighbouring areas of the somatosensory cortex take over the region that served the missing limb
nodes.note: Spinal sensitization and abnormal firing from cut nerve endings add to it. The more the cortex remaps, the worse the pain.

nodes.q: He is started on gabapentin. Which channel subunit does it bind?
nodes.a: The alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels
nodes.note: Binding reduces calcium entry and release of excitatory transmitters from sensitized neurons. Tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline are the other first-line neuropathic pain drugs; opioids and simple analgesics work poorly.

nodes.q: Which non-drug treatment retrains the brain?
nodes.note: Watching the intact limb move in a mirror gives the brain visual feedback that the missing limb is moving.

nodes.q: Shooting pains could suggest a stump neuroma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pain at the residual limb scar with a tender nodule that reproduces the pain when tapped (Tinel sign)**
**Pain felt in the absent foot; the stump itself is non-tender**

nodes.note: The trap: both follow nerve injury at the amputation.

nodes.q: Pain after surgery could suggest chronic infection of the residual limb. How do you tell them apart?

split.a: Chronic infection of the residual limb
split.note: **Pain in the stump with redness, warmth, drainage and fever**
**Healed non-tender stump, no fever, pain in the missing foot**

nodes.q: Shooting leg pain could suggest radiculitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Back pain radiating along a dermatome of the remaining limb, with a positive straight-leg raise**
**No back pain; pain felt in the part that is gone**

nodes.q: Chronic pain could suggest fibromyalgia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Widespread aching with fatigue, poor sleep and multiple tender points, mostly in women**
**Pain confined to the missing limb after an amputation**

nodes.q: The episodes could suggest a neuralgia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Paroxysmal stabbing pain along the course of a nerve in a body part that is still there, often with a trigger**
**Pain felt in a limb that has been removed, worse with anxiety and temperature**

root.stem: A 50-year-old man is brought in by his wife because of personality changes over 2 years and worse thinking over the last 3 months. He was a quiet, courteous accountant, but now he shouts at strangers, makes crude jokes, eats sweets compulsively, and nearly put the family's savings into a risky start-up. His speech has become less fluent. He still finds his way home and remembers recent family events. He has no tremor, no involuntary jerking movements and no history of strokes. His father had similar changes at age 55. A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shows marked atrophy of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes with the parietal lobes spared.
root.oneliner: 50M + 2 years of personality change, shouting at strangers, crude jokes, compulsive eating, near-ruinous investment + 3 months of cognitive decline, less fluent speech + memory and navigation intact + no tremor, no jerking movements, no strokes + father similar at 55 + frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, parietal spared
highlight: nearly put the family's savings into a risky start-up
still finds his way home and remembers recent family events
no tremor, no involuntary jerking movements and no history of strokes
father had similar changes at age 55
atrophy of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes with the parietal lobes spared

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A neurodegenerative dementia of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes, often starting before age 65. The clincher: **personality change and disinhibition before memory loss, with frontal and anterior temporal atrophy**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: An older name the exam still uses as an answer for this syndrome. Strictly, Pick disease is the subtype with Pick bodies.

nodes.q: Which microscopic finding marks Pick disease?
nodes.a: Pick bodies: round, silver-staining, tau-positive inclusions in neurons
nodes.note: Ballooned neurons (Pick cells) are also seen. Other forms contain inclusions of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) instead of tau.

nodes.q: Damage to which part of the frontal lobe explains his disinhibition and crude, socially inappropriate behaviour?
nodes.note: Orbitofrontal damage releases social behaviour from control (disinhibition, poor judgment). Dorsolateral prefrontal damage instead causes apathy and poor planning (executive dysfunction). His scan shows the frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with the parietal lobes spared, unlike the temporoparietal and hippocampal atrophy of Alzheimer disease.

nodes.q: Which gene, through an expanded hexanucleotide repeat, is the most common familial cause?
nodes.note: The same expansion causes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and some families have both. Other familial forms involve the tau gene (MAPT) and progranulin (GRN). Many cases are autosomal dominant, as his father's early illness suggests.

nodes.q: Which drug group helps his disinhibition and compulsions?
nodes.note: Cholinesterase inhibitors do not help and can worsen behavior. No drug slows the disease.

nodes.q: His cognitive decline could suggest Alzheimer disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Memory loss and getting lost first, personality preserved early**; amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles; temporoparietal atrophy
**Personality change and disinhibition first, with memory and navigation intact**; frontal and anterior temporal atrophy

nodes.note: The trap: both cause progressive dementia in the sixth decade.

nodes.q: His family history could suggest Huntington disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Chorea with behavioral change, CAG repeat expansion on chromosome 4, caudate atrophy**
**No involuntary jerking movements; frontal and temporal atrophy**

nodes.q: His decline could suggest vascular dementia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Stepwise worsening with vascular risk factors, focal deficits and multiple infarcts on imaging**
**Gradual decline, no strokes, focal lobar atrophy**

nodes.q: Late cognitive decline could suggest Parkinson disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Resting tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia; dementia, if any, appears late**
**No tremor; behavior changes first**

root.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 12 hours of fever, vomiting, refusal to eat and irritability. He has not had any routine vaccines since his 2-month visit. His temperature is 39.9°C (103.8°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. His neck is stiff and he resists flexion. There is no rash. A lumbar puncture yields cloudy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with many neutrophils, a high protein concentration and a low glucose concentration, and gram-positive diplococci are seen on Gram stain.
root.oneliner: 2-year-old boy + 12 hours of fever, vomiting, irritability + no vaccines since 2 months + stiff neck + no rash + cloudy CSF with many neutrophils, high protein, low glucose + gram-positive diplococci
highlight: has not had any routine vaccines since his 2-month visit
neck is stiff and he resists flexion
many neutrophils, a high protein concentration and a low glucose concentration

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Infection of the meninges. The clincher: **fever and a stiff neck with cloudy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showing many neutrophils, high protein and low glucose**.

nodes.q: Which organism is the cause?
nodes.note: Encapsulated, alpha-hemolytic, lancet-shaped **gram-positive diplococci**; optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble. It is the most common cause in children over 1 month and in adults.

nodes.q: Which virulence factor lets it escape phagocytosis?
nodes.note: Antibodies against the capsule opsonize it so that the spleen can clear it.

nodes.q: Which enzyme helps it colonize the nasopharynx before it invades?
nodes.note: It cleaves secretory immunoglobulin A on mucosa. Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae make it too. The organism then enters the blood and crosses into the meninges.

nodes.q: Which type of vaccine protects an infant from it?
nodes.note: Linking the capsular polysaccharide to a protein carrier recruits T helper cells, giving class switching and memory B cells even under age 2. A plain polysaccharide vaccine (used in adults over 65) triggers a T-cell-independent response that does not work in infants. Toxoid vaccines (tetanus, diphtheria) target toxins, and recombinant vaccines (hepatitis B, human papillomavirus) use a single viral protein.

nodes.q: Which drugs are started at once, before the CSF results return?
nodes.a: Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, with dexamethasone given with or just before the first dose
nodes.note: Vancomycin covers penicillin-resistant pneumococci. Add ampicillin under 1 month of age or over 50 to cover Listeria. Dexamethasone lowers the risk of hearing loss and death.

nodes.q: Loss of which organ's function puts a patient at highest risk of overwhelming infection with this organism?
nodes.a: The spleen (asplenia, including the autosplenectomy of sickle cell disease)
nodes.note: The spleen clears opsonized encapsulated bacteria. These patients need the conjugate vaccine and prompt antibiotics for fever.

nodes.q: Which is the most common long-term complication?
nodes.note: Others: seizures, hydrocephalus and learning problems.

nodes.q: An unvaccinated toddler with meningitis could have Haemophilus influenzae type b. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Gram-negative coccobacilli; unvaccinated child**; prevented by the Hib conjugate vaccine
**Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci in the CSF**

nodes.note: The trap: both occur in toddlers with missing vaccines and give identical CSF.

nodes.q: Fever and a stiff neck in a child could suggest meningococcal meningitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Gram-negative diplococci + petechial or purpuric rash**; risk of adrenal hemorrhage; contacts get rifampin
**Gram-positive diplococci; no rash**

nodes.q: His fever and stiff neck could suggest viral meningitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Mostly lymphocytes in the CSF with normal glucose; milder illness**
**Many neutrophils, low glucose, high protein, and organisms on Gram stain**

nodes.q: Gram-positive organisms in the CSF could suggest Listeria. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Gram-positive rods with tumbling motility; newborns, adults over 50 and immunosuppressed patients**; treated with ampicillin
**Gram-positive diplococci in an unvaccinated toddler**

root.stem: An 18-year-old man has mild intellectual disability and has had seizures since infancy, which began as clusters of sudden flexion jerks of the trunk and arms. His cheeks and nose are covered with small red-brown papules, and a Wood lamp shows several pale, leaf-shaped patches on his trunk. An echocardiogram in infancy showed a heart mass that later shrank. An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan shows multiple bilateral kidney masses with fat density. A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shows several firm nodules in the cerebral cortex and small calcified nodules along the walls of the lateral ventricles. His mother has similar facial papules and seizures.
root.oneliner: 18M + seizures since infancy, began as flexion-jerk clusters + mild intellectual disability + red-brown facial papules + pale leaf-shaped patches under Wood lamp + infant heart mass that shrank + bilateral fat-density kidney masses + cortical nodules and calcified periventricular nodules + mother similar
highlight: multiple bilateral kidney masses with fat density
firm nodules in the cerebral cortex
small calcified nodules along the walls of the lateral ventricles
His mother has similar facial papules and seizures

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome with hamartomas in many organs. The clincher: **seizures + intellectual disability + red-brown facial papules + hamartomas in brain, kidney and heart**.

nodes.q: Which pale skin lesions, best seen under a Wood lamp, are often the earliest sign?
nodes.note: He also has facial angiofibromas (the red-brown papules, once called adenoma sebaceum). Shagreen patches over the lower back and fibromas around the nails are other skin signs.

nodes.q: Which genes are mutated?
nodes.note: Both are tumor suppressors; inheritance is autosomal dominant, as in his mother, though most cases are new mutations. TSC2 lies next to PKD1, so a deletion of both causes tuberous sclerosis with polycystic kidneys.

nodes.q: Which growth pathway do these proteins normally restrain?
nodes.a: The mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) pathway
nodes.note: Loss lets cells grow unchecked and form hamartomas.

nodes.q: What type of lesion are the firm nodules in his cerebral cortex?
nodes.note: A hamartoma is a disorganized overgrowth of tissue native to the site. Tubers cause the seizures and intellectual disability.

nodes.q: Which seizure type did the flexion-jerk clusters of his infancy represent?
nodes.note: Tuberous sclerosis is a leading cause. Vigabatrin is the first-line drug in this setting; adrenocorticotropic hormone is used for other causes.

nodes.q: Which tumor can grow from the ventricular nodules and block the foramen of Monro?
nodes.note: It grows slowly from a subependymal nodule near the foramen of Monro and causes obstructive hydrocephalus of the lateral ventricles. It is the classic central nervous system tumor of this disease.

nodes.q: Which kidney lesions are found in most patients?
nodes.note: Benign tumors of abnormal blood vessels, smooth muscle and fat. Large ones (over about 4 cm) can bleed massively into the retroperitoneum. Women may also develop lymphangioleiomyomatosis of the lung, a related smooth-muscle proliferation.

nodes.q: Which infant heart tumor is the earliest sign?
nodes.note: Often regresses with age.

nodes.q: Which drug group shrinks the kidney and ventricular tumors?
nodes.note: They block the pathway that is overactive in this disease.

nodes.q: His kidney masses could suggest von Hippel-Lindau disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas + clear cell renal carcinoma**; VHL gene on chromosome 3
**Fat-density angiomyolipomas + cortical tubers + facial angiofibromas**

nodes.note: The trap: both are dominant syndromes with bilateral kidney tumors and brain lesions.

nodes.q: His skin lesions could suggest neurofibromatosis type 1. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Six or more café-au-lait spots, cutaneous neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic glioma**
**Ash-leaf patches and facial angiofibromas with cortical tubers**

nodes.q: Seizures with a facial skin lesion could suggest Sturge-Weber syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Port-wine stain in the ophthalmic (V1) distribution + leptomeningeal angioma with tram-track calcification**
**Facial papules (angiofibromas), not a flat stain; tubers and subependymal nodules**

nodes.q: A brain lesion in a young man with seizures could suggest a primary brain tumor such as glioblastoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Single enhancing mass with a necrotic center in an older adult; no skin or kidney findings**
**Multiple small hamartomas with skin, heart and kidney lesions and a family history**

root.stem: A 58-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter for 4 years of slowly worsening memory. She now forgets her grandchildren's names, has trouble finding words and objects such as her glasses, gets lost in her own neighbourhood, and thinks the wrong person is president. She is pleasant and cooperative, scores 19 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, and has no weakness, tremor, hallucinations or day-to-day swings in alertness. Vibration sense in her feet is normal. Her father and brother both developed memory loss in their fifties. Head imaging shows widened cortical sulci and enlarged ventricles. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 are normal, and she has no incontinence or gait problem.
root.oneliner: 58F + 4 years of slow memory loss from age 54 + word-finding trouble, gets lost + 19/30 on Mini-Mental State Examination + no focal weakness, tremor, hallucinations or fluctuations + father and brother with memory loss in their fifties + wide sulci, big ventricles on imaging + normal thyroid-stimulating hormone and B12 + no gait or bladder problem
highlight: gets lost in her own neighbourhood
no weakness, tremor, hallucinations or day-to-day swings in alertness
Vibration sense in her feet is normal
father and brother both developed memory loss in their fifties
widened cortical sulci and enlarged ventricles

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common cause of dementia. The clincher: **gradual loss of recent memory over years, followed by word-finding trouble and getting lost, with cortical shrinkage and no focal weakness**. Onset in her early fifties with an affected father and brother points to the early-onset familial form.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease; exam options often use this one.

nodes.q: After recent memory fails, which three deficits appear as the disease advances?
nodes.a: Aphasia (word-finding trouble), apraxia and visuospatial disorientation (getting lost)
nodes.note: Remote memories, personality and motor function are kept until late. She is pleasant and cooperative, as these patients often are early on.

nodes.q: Which two microscopic findings define it at autopsy?
nodes.a: Neuritic plaques outside neurons and neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons
nodes.note: Neuritic plaques are extracellular; neurofibrillary tangles are intracellular. Neuron loss is greatest in the hippocampus and cerebral cortex. In life, amyloid positron emission tomography or cerebrospinal fluid markers support the diagnosis; autopsy confirms it.

nodes.q: Which protein forms the core of the plaques?
nodes.a: Beta-amyloid, cut from amyloid precursor protein
nodes.note: Amyloid precursor protein is cut by beta-secretase and then gamma-secretase. Too much of the 42-amino-acid fragment (amyloid beta 42) clumps into plaques. Normal cutting by alpha-secretase gives no amyloid.

nodes.q: Which protein forms the tangles, and in what chemical state?
nodes.a: Tau, a microtubule-associated protein, in a hyperphosphorylated state
nodes.note: Hyperphosphorylated tau detaches from microtubules and aggregates as paired helical filaments. The number of tangles tracks the severity of dementia better than the number of plaques.

nodes.q: Beta-amyloid also builds up in the walls of small cortical arteries. Which bleed does this cause in older adults?
nodes.a: Recurrent lobar intracerebral hemorrhage (cerebral amyloid angiopathy)
nodes.note: Lobar (cortical-subcortical) bleeds, unlike the deep basal ganglia bleeds of hypertension. Congo red shows apple-green birefringence in the vessel walls.

nodes.q: Her father and brother were also affected in their fifties. Which gene is most often mutated in this early-onset familial form?
nodes.note: Autosomal dominant. Presenilin 1 (chromosome 14) is most common, then presenilin 2 (chromosome 1) and amyloid precursor protein (chromosome 21). All raise production of amyloid beta 42.

nodes.q: Why do people with Down syndrome get this dementia early?
nodes.a: They have three copies of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21
nodes.note: Nearly all show plaques and tangles by age 40, and most develop dementia in their fifties or sixties.

nodes.q: Which gene variant raises the risk of the common late-onset form the most?
nodes.note: Apolipoprotein E is on chromosome 19. One epsilon 4 copy raises risk about threefold, two copies much more. The epsilon 2 allele is protective. Age is the strongest risk factor overall.

nodes.q: Which brain regions shrink first?
nodes.a: The entorhinal cortex and hippocampus (medial temporal lobe), then the temporal and parietal cortex
nodes.note: This explains why recent memory goes first and why she gets lost.

nodes.q: Her brain imaging shows widened sulci and enlarged ventricles. What explains the large ventricles?
nodes.note: Brain tissue is lost and cerebrospinal fluid fills the empty space. Pressure is normal and there is no blockage, unlike true hydrocephalus.

nodes.q: Which neurons are lost early, causing low acetylcholine in the cortex?
nodes.a: Cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert in the basal forebrain
nodes.note: The nucleus basalis of Meynert sends acetylcholine to the whole cerebral cortex and its activity depends on choline acetyltransferase, which falls early. This loss is the target of cholinesterase inhibitor therapy.

nodes.q: Which drug class gives a modest benefit in mild to moderate disease?
nodes.note: Donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine slow decline for a time but do not stop the disease. Newer anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) are used in early disease and can cause brain swelling or microbleeds (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities).

nodes.q: How does donepezil work at the synapse?
nodes.a: It blocks acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine lasts longer in the synaptic cleft
nodes.note: More acetylcholine reaches cortical receptors. It does not block choline reuptake or stop acetylcholine release.

nodes.q: Which heart rhythm adverse effect should be watched for?
nodes.note: Extra vagal tone also causes nausea, diarrhea and vivid dreams.

nodes.q: Memantine is added in moderate to severe disease. Which receptor does it block?
nodes.a: The N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor (an uncompetitive antagonist)
nodes.note: It limits excitotoxic calcium entry into neurons. Adverse effects: dizziness, confusion, headache.

nodes.q: Which two reversible causes of dementia do her normal blood tests rule out?
nodes.note: Check both before labelling the case Alzheimer disease. Syphilis, depression (pseudodementia) and drug effects are other reversible causes.

nodes.q: What is the usual end stage and cause of death?
nodes.a: Severe dementia, loss of speech and walking, and death from aspiration pneumonia or infection
nodes.note: Average survival is about 8 to 10 years from diagnosis.

nodes.q: Her enlarged ventricles could suggest normal pressure hydrocephalus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Gait problem first, then **urinary incontinence and dementia (wet, wobbly, wacky)**; ventricles large with tight, not wide, sulci; improves after lumbar puncture
**Memory loss first**, no early gait or bladder problem; ventricles large because of **wide sulci and cortical shrinkage**

nodes.note: Both show enlarged ventricles on imaging.

nodes.q: Her memory loss could suggest vascular dementia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Stepwise decline with hypertension and focal signs**; magnetic resonance imaging shows multiple lacunar infarcts
**Smooth gradual decline with no focal signs**; magnetic resonance imaging shows global cortical and hippocampal shrinkage

nodes.q: Her memory loss and confusion could suggest Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Dementia over **weeks to months with startle myoclonus**; spongiform change without plaques or tangles
Dementia over **years** with **plaques and tangles** and no myoclonus early

nodes.q: Her word-finding trouble could suggest frontotemporal dementia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Onset 45 to 65; **personality change, disinhibition or language loss first**, memory spared early; frontal and temporal atrophy; **Pick bodies** (round tau inclusions)
**Memory loss first**, behaviour and personality kept (she is pleasant and cooperative); plaques and tangles

nodes.note: The trap: both can start in the fifties, and she has word-finding trouble.

nodes.q: Her slowly progressive dementia could suggest dementia with Lewy bodies. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Well-formed visual hallucinations, day-to-day fluctuations in alertness and parkinsonism** within a year of the dementia; alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in the cortex; severe sensitivity to antipsychotics
**Memory loss first with no hallucinations, fluctuations or tremor**; plaques and tangles

nodes.q: Her memory loss could suggest vitamin B12 deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Megaloblastic anemia, loss of vibration and position sense, and spasticity (subacute combined degeneration)**; low B12 with raised methylmalonic acid; reversible with B12
**Normal B12 and normal vibration sense**; progressive memory loss with cortical atrophy

root.stem: A 58-year-old woman has had a year of episodes in which her left leg and foot jerk rhythmically for about 3 minutes, plus headaches that have grown steadily worse over 6 months. Her left ankle jerk is brisk and a Babinski sign is present on the left. She is otherwise healthy, has no cancer history, no immune disorder and no recent fever. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a single 2-cm, round, enhancing mass attached to the right side of the falx near the central sulcus, with a thin enhancing tail along the dura, and the brain is pushed away from the mass. She has had no skin lesions or hearing loss, and a chest film is normal.
root.oneliner: 58F + 1 year of rhythmic left leg jerking lasting 3 minutes + progressive headaches + brisk left ankle jerk, left Babinski + single 2-cm round enhancing mass on the right side of the falx with dural tail, brain pushed away + healthy, no cancer, immune disorder or fever
highlight: left leg and foot jerk rhythmically for about 3 minutes
headaches that have grown steadily worse
Babinski sign is present on the left
no cancer history, no immune disorder
single 2-cm, round, enhancing mass attached to the right side of the falx
thin enhancing tail along the dura
the brain is pushed away from the mass

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A slow-growing, benign tumour of the meninges. The clincher: **an enhancing, round, dural-based mass outside the brain (extra-axial) in a middle-aged woman**.

nodes.q: Her mass is attached to the falx with a dural tail and pushes the brain away. Where does that place it?
nodes.note: It compresses the brain rather than invading it. Intra-axial tumours (gliomas, metastases, lymphoma) sit inside the brain.

nodes.q: From which cell does it arise?
nodes.note: They lie in the arachnoid villi and granulations. The exam option is often written as 'meningeal'.

nodes.q: Which two microscopic features are classic?
nodes.a: Whorled sheets of cells and psammoma bodies (round calcified deposits)
nodes.note: Psammoma bodies are also seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian tumours and mesothelioma.

nodes.q: What World Health Organization grade are most of these tumours?
nodes.a: Grade 1: benign, slow-growing and well circumscribed
nodes.note: Rare atypical (grade 2) and anaplastic (grade 3) types recur and invade.

nodes.q: Which inherited syndrome predisposes to multiple meningiomas?
nodes.note: Loss of the merlin gene on chromosome 22; bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the other hallmark. Other risk factors: female sex, prior cranial radiation. Tumour cells often carry progesterone receptors, and growth can speed up in pregnancy.

nodes.q: Why do rhythmic jerks affect only her left leg?
nodes.a: The tumour presses on the right motor cortex leg area on the medial surface next to the falx
nodes.note: The leg lies on the medial precentral gyrus, so a parasagittal mass causes focal motor seizures of the opposite leg, with upper motor neuron signs (brisk reflex, Babinski sign) on that side.

nodes.q: A 50-year-old woman with 6 months of spastic weakness of all four limbs and bilateral Babinski signs has a 1.5-cm, well-defined round mass indenting the cervical cord at C1. Which compartment of the spinal canal does a meningioma there occupy?
nodes.a: Intradural extramedullary (inside the dura, outside the cord)
nodes.note: It indents the cord and gives upper motor neuron signs below the level. Spinal meningiomas mostly affect women and occur most often in the thoracic spine; with schwannoma they are the leading intradural extramedullary tumours.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment of a symptomatic tumour?
nodes.note: Small asymptomatic tumours can be watched with serial imaging. Radiosurgery treats residual or inaccessible tumour.

nodes.q: Which drug reduces the swelling around the tumour before surgery?
nodes.note: A corticosteroid that lowers vasogenic oedema.

nodes.q: What predicts recurrence after surgery?
nodes.a: Incomplete removal or a higher grade (atypical or anaplastic)
nodes.note: The dural attachment is removed with the tumour to lower the risk.

nodes.q: Her mass could be a metastatic carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Multiple intra-axial lesions at the grey-white junction** with surrounding oedema and a known primary (lung, breast, melanoma)
**Single, round, dural-based extra-axial mass** with a dural tail and a 1-year course

nodes.note: The closest look-alike because it also enhances.

nodes.q: Her enhancing brain mass could suggest an astrocytoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Intra-axial infiltrating mass** inside the brain, ill-defined edges; glial fibrillary acidic protein-positive glial cells; glioblastoma shows necrosis with pseudopalisading
**Extra-axial, well-defined, dural-based**, with psammoma bodies

nodes.q: Her enhancing brain mass could suggest an oligodendroglioma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Mostly **frontal white matter with calcifications**; round cells with a clear halo ('fried egg'); co-deletion of chromosome arms 1p and 19q
**Dural-based extra-axial mass on the falx** with whorls and psammoma bodies

nodes.q: Her enhancing brain mass could suggest primary central nervous system lymphoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Immunocompromised host (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) with Epstein-Barr virus**; deep periventricular mass, often crossing the corpus callosum
**Immune-competent woman; extra-axial mass at the falx**; slow, years-long course

nodes.q: Her cervical mass could suggest an epidural abscess. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, severe focal back pain and a raised white cell count** over days, often after infection or injection drug use; rim-enhancing collection
**Painless, afebrile, slow course over months with a round well-defined mass**

nodes.q: Her cervical cord compression could suggest a herniated disc. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Acute or recurrent **radicular pain** from a disc fragment, mostly lumbar or lower cervical (C5 to C7); not a round mass at C1
**Slow cord compression from a round extramedullary mass at the top of the cervical cord**

nodes.q: Her cervical mass could suggest a spinal cord astrocytoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Intramedullary**: expands the cord itself with ill-defined edges, often with a syrinx; early dissociated sensory loss
**Extramedullary, well-defined round mass that indents the cord from outside**

title: Focal impaired awareness seizure (complex partial seizure)

root.stem: A 39-year-old woman is seen for 8 months of spells that come without any trigger. Before each one she smells a foul burning odour that her husband cannot smell. During the interview she stops talking mid-sentence, turns her head to the left and stiffens her left arm, with a blank look and no response to questions. She then smacks her lips and picks at her clothes. The spell lasts about 40 seconds, and she takes 4 to 5 minutes to return to normal. Once, a spell ended with her whole body stiffening and then jerking for 2 minutes; she bit her tongue and was confused for 20 minutes afterward. She had a prolonged seizure with a high fever at age 2. She drinks alcohol only rarely, drives to work every day and asks whether she may keep driving.
root.oneliner: 39F + 8 months of unprovoked spells + foul burning smell before each + stops talking, head turn, arm stiffening, blank look, unresponsive + lip smacking and picking + 40 seconds then 4 to 5 minutes of confusion + once whole-body stiffening then jerking with tongue bite + prolonged febrile seizure at age 2 + rare alcohol + asks about driving
highlight: smells a foul burning odour that her husband cannot smell
blank look and no response to questions
smacks her lips and picks at her clothes
4 to 5 minutes to return to normal
whole body stiffening and then jerking for 2 minutes
prolonged seizure with a high fever at age 2
asks whether she may keep driving

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A seizure that starts in one area of the brain and impairs awareness. The clincher: **blank stare with loss of responsiveness, lip smacking and hand picking, then slow confusion for minutes afterward**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The older term; both names describe the same seizure type.

nodes.q: She has had repeated spells over 8 months with no trigger. What chronic disorder does this define?
nodes.note: Epilepsy means two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, or one with a high risk of recurrence. Provoked seizures (low sodium, low glucose, alcohol withdrawal, fever) do not count.

nodes.q: What are the lip smacking and hand picking called?
nodes.note: Repeated, purposeless movements during impaired awareness. Head turning and arm stiffening on one side can come first.

nodes.q: She smells a foul odour that no one else notices just before each episode. Which lobe does this aura point to?
nodes.note: The aura is itself a focal aware seizure (formerly simple partial) starting in the limbic temporal cortex near the uncus. Other temporal auras are déjà vu, a rising epigastric feeling and fear.

nodes.q: One spell ended with whole-body stiffening, then jerking, a bitten tongue and 20 minutes of confusion. What is this seizure type called?
nodes.a: Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizure)
nodes.note: The discharge spread from the temporal focus to both hemispheres. The tonic phase (stiffening) comes before the clonic phase (jerking); the confusion afterward is the postictal state. The smell was the warning before it spread.

nodes.q: If a convulsion like this lasts longer than 5 minutes, what is it called?
nodes.note: Untreated it causes hypoxic brain injury, rhabdomyolysis and death. The old definition was 30 minutes; treatment now starts at 5 minutes.

nodes.q: Which drug class is given first for status epilepticus?
nodes.note: Benzodiazepines raise how often the gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) chloride channel opens. Intramuscular midazolam if there is no line; then fosphenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam.

nodes.q: She had a prolonged febrile seizure at age 2. Which structural change in the temporal lobe is the usual cause of her spells?
nodes.note: Neuron loss and gliosis in the hippocampus (especially the CA1 sector), seen as a small bright hippocampus on magnetic resonance imaging.

nodes.q: Which test shows the seizure focus?
nodes.a: Electroencephalogram with sharp waves over the anterior temporal region
nodes.note: Magnetic resonance imaging looks for hippocampal sclerosis or a tumour.

nodes.q: Which drugs are first line for focal seizures?
nodes.a: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam; carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine are alternatives
nodes.note: Valproate is avoided in women who may become pregnant (neural tube defects). Lamotrigine is preferred in women of childbearing age.

nodes.q: Her doctor chooses carbamazepine. How does it work?
nodes.a: It blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and prolongs their inactivated state
nodes.note: This stops high-frequency repetitive firing of neurons. Phenytoin, oxcarbazepine and lamotrigine act the same way.

nodes.q: Which blood count problem needs monitoring on carbamazepine?
nodes.note: Other classic adverse effects: hyponatremia (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (highest risk with human leukocyte antigen B*15:02 in people of Asian ancestry), induction of cytochrome P450 enzymes (lowers oral contraceptive levels) and neural tube defects in pregnancy.

nodes.q: She asks whether she may keep driving. What is the rule?
nodes.a: She may not drive until she has been seizure-free for the interval set by her state (usually 3 to 12 months)
nodes.note: Once that interval has passed she is medically qualified to drive, even while she keeps taking an antiseizure drug such as carbamazepine; a person seizure-free for years on treatment may drive. No repeat electroencephalogram is required first, and a 10-year wait is not the rule. Physicians should know whether their state requires them to report.

nodes.q: What is offered when two drugs fail?
nodes.note: Surgery gives the best seizure freedom when the focus is in one temporal lobe.

nodes.q: Her staring spell could suggest an absence seizure. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Child, **5 to 10 seconds of staring with no automatisms and no postictal confusion**; 3-hertz spike-and-wave on electroencephalogram; ethosuximide
Adult, **30 seconds to 2 minutes with lip smacking and a 4 to 5 minute confusion afterward**

nodes.note: The trap: both begin with a blank stare.

nodes.q: Her head turning and arm stiffening could suggest a simple partial motor seizure. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Awareness is kept** while one part of the body jerks (Jacksonian march)
**Awareness is lost**, she does not respond to questions and recovers slowly

nodes.q: Her smell before each spell could suggest a simple partial sensory seizure alone. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Awareness is kept** and the event stops at the sensation (tingling, a flash of light or a smell); her aura on its own is one
**Awareness is lost** with automatisms and postictal confusion

nodes.q: Her one whole-body episode could suggest convulsive syncope. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Trigger (standing, pain, heat), pallor, a few seconds of jerks and recovery within a minute**; no tongue biting
**Smell aura, stiffening then jerking for 2 minutes, a bitten tongue, then 20 minutes of confusion**

nodes.note: The trap: both can cause jerking with loss of consciousness.

nodes.q: Her seizures could be provoked by alcohol withdrawal. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Heavy daily drinking stopped 6 to 48 hours earlier**, with tremor and autonomic overactivity; not epilepsy
**She drinks only rarely**, and her spells come without any trigger, each with the same smell aura

root.stem: A 2-year-old boy was born at 29 weeks after a complicated pregnancy. He sat up late, at 8 months, and now crawls by dragging his legs behind him. His leg muscles are stiff with brisk knee reflexes, his legs cross like scissors when he is lifted, and his right hip has an early adduction contracture with subluxation. His arms are less affected, muscle bulk looks normal, his creatine kinase is normal and he has not lost any skills he once had. His surgeons plan an operation to relieve the contracture.
root.oneliner: 2M + born at 29 weeks + sat up at 8 months, crawls dragging legs + stiff legs, brisk knee reflexes, scissoring + right hip adduction contracture with subluxation + arms less affected, normal bulk and creatine kinase + no regression

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A non-progressive motor disorder from a fixed brain injury in the fetus or infant. The clincher: **delayed motor milestones with spasticity, brisk reflexes and no regression, after a premature birth**.

nodes.q: He has not lost any skills he once had. What does this say about the brain injury?
nodes.a: It is fixed and non-progressive, although the movement problems change as he grows
nodes.note: A child who loses skills (regression) needs another diagnosis, such as a degenerative or muscle disease.

nodes.q: His legs are stiff and his arms are less affected. Which type of cerebral palsy is this?
nodes.note: Spastic types (upper motor neuron signs) are the most common. Dyskinetic (athetoid) cerebral palsy follows kernicterus or basal ganglia injury; hemiplegic follows perinatal stroke.

nodes.q: Which birth history is the strongest risk factor?
nodes.a: Prematurity with brain injury (the most common cause)
nodes.note: Others: birth asphyxia, intrauterine infection, kernicterus and perinatal stroke.

nodes.q: Which white matter lesion of premature infants explains why his legs are worse than his arms?
nodes.note: White matter injury beside the lateral ventricles, often after intraventricular hemorrhage or hypoperfusion. The corticospinal fibres to the legs pass closest to the ventricles.

nodes.q: His surgeons plan to relieve the hip adduction contracture. Cutting which nerve to the adductor muscles would do this?
nodes.note: The obturator nerve (L2 to L4) supplies adductor longus, brevis and magnus (adductor part) and gracilis. Obturator neurectomy or adductor tendon lengthening eases the adduction.

nodes.q: Untreated, what does his hip subluxation progress to?
nodes.note: Unbalanced adductor and flexor pull drives the femoral head out. Hip imaging is repeated through childhood.

nodes.q: Which approach treats it overall?
nodes.a: Physical and occupational therapy plus drugs for spasticity
nodes.note: Drugs: baclofen, diazepam and botulinum toxin injections; orthopaedic surgery and selective dorsal rhizotomy in selected children.

nodes.q: How does diazepam reduce spasticity?
nodes.a: It binds its own site on the gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) receptor and raises how often the chloride channel opens when GABA is bound
nodes.note: It is a positive allosteric modulator and cannot open the channel without GABA. Barbiturates instead lengthen the opening time.

nodes.q: How does baclofen work?
nodes.a: It is an agonist at the gamma-aminobutyric acid type B (GABA-B) receptor
nodes.note: A G-protein-coupled receptor; it reduces release of excitatory transmitters in the spinal cord.

nodes.q: How does botulinum toxin help a spastic muscle?
nodes.a: It blocks release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
nodes.note: The effect lasts about 3 months.

nodes.q: Delayed milestones in a boy could suggest Duchenne muscular dystrophy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Floppy, weak muscles, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gowers sign, raised creatine kinase and regression**; reflexes reduced
**Stiff muscles, brisk reflexes and no regression**; muscle bulk and creatine kinase normal

nodes.q: Difficulty with sitting could suggest spinal muscular atrophy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hypotonia with absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations**; progressive; survival motor neuron 1 gene deletion
**Spasticity with brisk reflexes**; non-progressive

nodes.note: The trap: both delay sitting.
